title: Regional and national burden and aetiologies of non-COVID lower respiratory infections in Latin America and the Caribbean, 1990-2023: a secondary analysis of the global burden of disease study 2023
abstract: Lower respiratory tract infections (LRTIs) remain a leading cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide, disproportionately affecting low- and middle-income regions. Reliable, up-to-date burden estimates are needed to inform public health strategies in Latin America and the Caribbean, where prevention and management strategies remain heterogeneous. We aimed to characterise temporal and geographical patterns in LRTI mortality, incidence, disability-adjusted life-years (DALYs), and aetiology across the region from 1990 to 2023. We analysed secondary, modelled estimates of mortality, incidence, and DALYs attributable to LRTIs in Latin America and the Caribbean from 1990 to 2023, extracted from the GBD 2023 Results Tool and produced following the standardised GBD protocol coordinated by the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation (IHME). In Latin America and the Caribbean, LRTI mortality declined in most countries between 1990 and 2023, with the steepest reductions among children younger than five years (e.g., Brazil ARC -6·16, 95% UI -6·61 to -5·71). All-age mortality rose in some countries, but age-standardised rates showed that these increases reflected population ageing rather than rising age-specific risk. Following a sustained pre-pandemic decline, incidence showed and overall upward direction in the post-pandemic period across age groups, although the magnitude and statistical relevance of these changes varied by age and country, with the largest increase observed among children in Suriname (ARC +8·84, 95% UI +2·80 to +14·95).remained the leading cause of LRTI mortality in 2023 (7·68 per 100,000, 95% UI 7·11-8·24; ARC -2·70, 95% UI -2·96 to -2·45). LRTIs remain a major cause of death in the region, with substantial progress among children but persistent burden among older adults, driven by population ageing, and evidence of a post-pandemic increase in incidence. There is a great importance of combining clinical interventions with broader public health strategies addressing vaccination coverage, antimicrobial-resistance surveillance, nutrition, housing, and access to primary care, particularly in populations that have experienced less favourable trends. title: Oral and anal detection of Treponema pallidum DNA among transgender women and travestis with high-titre syphilis in Brazil: findings from the MyTTrA study
abstract: Data on transgender women and(TGW) concerning oral and anal detection of(TP) DNA are lacking. We aimed to estimate the prevalence of oral and anal TP DNA detection and the frequency of azithromycin resistance-associated mutations among TGW with high-titre syphilis in Brazil. We conducted a nested cross-sectional study as part of the TransOdara study among TGW in five Brazilian cities. Participants with high-titre syphilis (reactive treponemal test and VDRL titre ≥1:8) and an analysable oral or anal specimen underwent quantitative PCR targeting theandgenes to detect TP DNA. TP DNA-positive specimens were further analysed using nested PCR and Sanger sequencing to identify mutations associated with azithromycin resistance. Among the 249 participants with high-titre serological syphilis and analysable sample, TP DNA was detected in 25 (10.0%, 95% CI 6.6-14.5): 14 (5.6%) from the oral site only, 6 (2.4%) from the anal site only, and 5 (2.0%) from both sites. Participants in whom TP DNA was detected were younger and more frequently reported STI symptoms and anogenital ulcers during the preceding six months. The detection rate increased with VDRL titre (odds ratio 2.44, 95% CI 1.74-3.41 per doubling of titre for any oral or anal detection). Mutations associated with azithromycin resistance were observed in 76% (19/25, 95% CI 54.9-90.6) of participants in whom TP was detected. TP DNA was detected in 10% of participants with high-titre serological syphilis. Detection increased with higher VDRL titres, supporting an association between higher non-treponemal titres and mucosal TP DNA detection. These findings support continued epidemiological and molecular surveillance of syphilis and of azithromycin resistance in transgender populations. They do not support site-specific PCR screening: syphilis diagnosis remains serological, and benzathine benzylpenicillin G remains the treatment of choice. title: Harnessing gasotransmitters for orthopaedic infection therapy: Mechanisms and advanced delivery platforms
abstract: Orthopaedic infections are increasingly prevalent in the aging population, posing a significant clinical and economic burden. Despite progress in antimicrobial therapies, challenges such as antibiotic resistance and superbug emergence persist. Gas therapy has emerged as a promising strategy for managing orthopaedic infections. Classical gasotransmitters-including nitric oxide (NO), carbon monoxide (CO), and hydrogen sulfide (HS)-exhibit antibacterial and immunomodulatory effects at controlled concentrations, though improper dosing may induce adverse effects. This review critically examines the dual mechanisms through which gasotransmitters combat infection while promoting orthopaedic regeneration. We also survey advanced delivery platforms-such as smart scaffolds, nano-reservoirs, and on-demand release systems-engineered for targeted gasotransmitter delivery to infected bone tissue. Finally, we discuss current limitations and future prospects, aiming to inspire novel biomaterial designs for targeted therapeutic delivery and to advance gas therapy as a viable option for orthopaedic infection treatment.

title: Bioprinted core-shell living material platform for spatially controlled encapsulation of Bacillus subtilis and sustained metabolite exchange
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) represents an escalating global health crisis, demanding alternative strategies to reduce resistant pathogen burden across environments. Microbe-based biocontrol is promising, yet effectively deploying it in practical settings remains challenging. In this study, we present a 3D bioprinted core-shell construct featuring a polyethylene glycol diacrylate (PEGDA) shell with tunable nanoscale porosity, encapsulating germinable spores of the biocontrol agentTH035. This configuration supports long-term spore viability while providing protection from common environmental stressors including UV-C irradiation, ethanol exposure, and desiccation over 4 weeks. The nanoporous PEGDA shell enables effective bacterial confinement while facilitating sufficient metabolite exchange forgermination and growth, as well as suppression of methicillin-resistant(MRSA) growth by approximately one order of magnitude. This approach demonstrates the feasibility of embeddingspores within engineered scaffolds for extended competitive functionality. The versatility and scalability of digital light processing (DLP) based bioprinting offers significant potential for tailored designs and high-throughput manufacturing. This proof-of-concept platform may find future applications in areas such as biomedical packaging, environmental sanitation, and built environment surface coatings, particularly in settings where intermittent moisture or nutrient availability can support spore germination and biocontrol activity.

title: Artificial intelligence catalyzes antimicrobial peptide design
abstract: With broad-spectrum, low resistance, and multifunctional properties, antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) are promising therapeutic agents against drug-resistant pathogens, yet their discovery and optimization still remain challenging due to the complexity of sequence-function associations. Artificial intelligence (AI), through the construction of comprehensive data-driven models that assisted with miscellaneous learning strategies, enables de novo peptide design by learning latent representations inherent in peptide sequences as well as their biological properties to ensure physically plausible and biologically relevant predictions. Consequently, this paradigm enhances the likelihood of designing peptide candidates with significantly improved therapeutic potential, reducing resource-intensive trial-and-error processes and revealing the transformative impact of computational innovation in advancing next-generation therapeutics. Here, we provide a snapshot of this field and survey two modes of AI-driven technologies for AMP design, one concentrated on identifying whether current data possess antimicrobial activity (identification-oriented) and the other on generating AMP candidates with potential therapeutic properties (generation-oriented). We also highlight the challenges and limitations that still hinder AMP development even accelerated by AI, as well as the foreseeable prospects, from finer-grained explorations to model-driven data enrichment and model enhancement.

title: Antifungal mechanisms of volatile organic compounds and lactic acid produced by Lactiplantibacillus pentosus and their biocontrol application in fresh corn against Fusarium graminearum
abstract: Fusarium graminearum causes cereal spoilage and mycotoxin production. Currently, biocontrol microorganisms have emerged as a safe and promising strategy to manage the contamination of toxin-producing fungi in cereal grains. The primary objective was to elucidate the antifungal mechanism of an isolated strain of Lactiplantibacillus pentosus Q11 against F. graminearum and to evaluate the preservative effects of its cell-free supernatant (CFS) in fresh sweet corn. In vitro antifungal assays of L. pentosus Q11 showed strong antagonistic activity against F. graminearum, Aspergillus flavus, and Penicillium expansum, as well as the ability to reduce zearalenone. Moreover, whole-genome analysis revealed no genes related to virulence and antimicrobial resistance, and no hemolytic activity was observed, which suggested the potential safety of strain Q11. Moreover, the CFS of L. pentosus Q11 effectively inhibited the mycelial growth of F. graminearum, disrupted hyphal integrity, and induced fungal cell death. Moreover, 3 organic acids and 38 volatile compounds in the CFS of Q11 strain were identified by SPME-GC-MS and HPLC, in which 2-nonanone, 2-methylpyrazine, lactic acid, acetic acid were predominant compounds. The CFS and lactic acid combined with 2-nonanone severely damaged hyphae of F. graminearum, by disrupting cell membrane and wall, leading to leakage of intracellular substances, showing a synergistic antifungal effect of the two vital compounds. Subsequently, the treatments of CFS and combined agents significantly decreased 88.05% - 89.52% of fungal populations, and AFBand DON mycotoxin accumulation in fresh sweet corn after 12 days of storage compared to the control. The malondialdehyde content in the treated corn was decreased by 29.25% - 31.50%, consistent with the higher activities of POD and APX, thereby preserving their sensory attributes and nutritional quality. Metabolomic analysis revealed that L-glutamate, γ-glutamylcysteine, and oxidized glutathione were significantly downregulated in the glutathione metabolism pathway in the treated corn, indicating that CFS containing lactic acid and 2-nonanone could repress fungal growth and alleviate oxidative stress in fresh sweet corn. Overall, these findings demonstrate that L. pentosus Q11 with synergistic volatile organic compounds and lactic acid is a promising biocontrol agent in preserving fresh sweet corn.

abstract: , a Gram-negative ESKAPE pathogen, has emerged as a challenging opportunistic pathogen in healthcare facilities due to its rapid acquisition of antimicrobial resistance. Carbapenem-resistant(CRAB) exhibits extensive multidrug resistance, creating an urgent need for novel therapeutics, making bacteriophage therapy a promising alternative. CRAB clinical isolate Ab3 was used as the host to screen bacteriophages. The isolated phage was comprehensively characterized through morphology, adsorption kinetics, one-step growth, lytic spectrum, anti-biofilm activity, stability testing, and complete genome sequencing with bioinformatics analysis. Jumbo phage AbIJP1, isolated from hospital sewage, represents the largest phage genome reported againstto date. It forms 6 -7 mm plaques; its virions have an icosahedral head (≈ 107 nm) and long contractile tail (≈ 280 nm). AbIJP1 exhibited high biphasic adsorption (>90% within 10 min), moderate burst size (57 PFU/bacterium), MOI-dependent bactericidal activity against CRAB, significant anti-biofilm property, and stability at 50 °C and pH 5-9. AbIJP1 was specific to, lysing 8/11 isolates by spot assay and productively infecting 7/11 by efficiency of plating (EOP), with no cross-species activity. Whole genome analysis revealed a 348,571 bp linear dsDNA genome (27% GC, 592 ORFs, 20 tRNAs) encoding morphogenesis, lysis, DNA replication and metabolism genes, with no lysogenic, antibiotic resistance or virulence genes. Taxonomic analysis placed AbIJP1 in a new genus of, with >99.8% of its genome distinct from known phages. Together with its lytic activity and genomic safety, these findings suggest the jumbo phage AbIJP1 is a promising therapeutic candidate against CRAB infections.

title: Buffalo farming in Nepal: current status, sustainability, value chains, and future development opportunities
abstract: Buffalo farming is central to Nepal's livestock sector, food supply, and rural livelihoods, yet the evidence on production, sustainability, health, and value chains remains fragmented. This structured narrative review synthesises peer-reviewed literature and authoritative national and international sources on buffalo production, genetic resources, nutrition, climate resilience, One Health, and value-chain development in Nepal. It emphasises evidence published since 2015 while retaining earlier foundational studies. Buffaloes contribute approximately 52.2% of national milk and 30.9% of meat production. Indigenous buffaloes, including Lime, Parkote, Gaddi, and Terai populations, represent important locally adapted genetic resources requiring conservation alongside productivity improvement. Crossbreeding with Murrah can increase productivity but must be accompanied by strategies to conserve indigenous genetic resources. Major constraints include seasonal feed deficits, reproductive inefficiency, heat stress, disease, limited performance recording, and weak value-chain infrastructure. Reports of multidrug-resistant bacteria and antimicrobial residues further highlight the need for integrated One Health surveillance and antimicrobial stewardship. Addressing these challenges requires improved feeding and breeding, preventive herd health, climate-resilient management, greater value addition, and enhanced food safety and traceability. Integrating productivity gains with genetic-resource conservation, environmental sustainability, and value-chain development is essential for the sustainable and resilient development of Nepal's buffalo sector.

title: A novel multidrug-resistant IncX1 plasmid in Salmonella Enteritidis: Co-carriage of bla (TEM-1B), sul2, aph(3″)-Ib, and aph(6)-id
abstract: serovar Enteritidis () remains a leading cause of global foodborne illness, with the emergence of multidrug-resistant (MDR)posing a serious threat to public health. Here, we report the characterization of a novel MDR IncX1 plasmid, designated SE-SDT01-P2 (24,483 bp), isolated fromSDT-01 (sequence type ST11). Whole-genome sequencing revealed that SE-SDT01-P2 co-harbors four clinically relevant antimicrobial resistance genes-,,, and-clustered within a unique 12-16 kbp resistance structural unit (RSU). The RSU is flanked by Tn3 transposon-associated elements and features a previously unreported duplication of an IS6-like element IS26 family transposase, herein named IS26(x2), resulting in a novel architecture: Tn3:: IS91:::: IS6-like element IS26 family transposase(x2). Conjugation experiments demonstrated that SE-SDT01-P2 is self-transmissible and capable of conferring ampicillin and sulfonamide resistance toJ53 recipients, with resistance levels influenced by host background. Comparative genomic analysis indicated cross-species dissemination potential, as highly similar plasmid backbones were identified inand. This study provides the first description of an IncX1 plasmid carrying that specific combination within a novel IS26-mediated RSU and underscores how MDR dissemination among zoonotic pathogens is accelerated by mobile genetic elements. These results highlight the pressing requirement for strengthened monitoring of resistance plasmids across the poultry production chain in order to reduce risks to public health.

Comprehensive safety and toxicity evaluation of Lactiplantibacillus plantarum LMT1-48, a potential probiotic strain isolated from Kimchi
abstract: Probiotics are widely commercialized as key ingredients in functional foods and dietary supplements; however, ensuring their safety is critical for consumers. In particular, safety must be carefully evaluated at the strain level, as both efficacy and potential risks can vary between strains. In this study, the safety of a novel probiotic strain,LMT1-48, was comprehensively evaluated using phenotypic, genomic, and toxicity studies. Minimum Inhibitory Concentration (MIC) values of all tested antibiotics were lower than the cut-off values of the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) guidelines.LMT1-48 did not exhibit hemolytic activity nor cytotoxicity. Production of harmful metabolites is also evaluated. The whole genome sequencing did not reveal any antibiotic resistance- or virulence-related genes. Neither single- nor repeated-dose oral toxicity studies have shown any treatment-related toxicological changes at any dose level. Overall, our results suggest thatLMT1-48 is a safe probiotic strain for human consumption.

title: Organic amendments and antibiotic resistance gene diversity in tropical agroecosystems of Réunion Island: an exploratory study
abstract: Environmental reservoirs of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) are increasingly recognized as important components of One Health surveillance. We explored antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) across agricultural environments on Réunion Island using high-throughput qPCR targeting 349 ARGs in 16 samples comprising manure, soils, water and vegetables. ARGs were widespread, with the highest richness and relative abundance in manure-amended soils and manure. ARG abundance was on average approximately 5-fold higher in amended than paired control soils. Among 60 ARGs classified as high risk to human health, 52 were detected, including 16 in water and 22 in raw vegetables. ARG profiles differed primarily among matrices. Antibiotic residues were detected in only five samples, and neither their occurrence nor Cu/Zn concentrations consistently mirrored ARG patterns. This exploratory screening identifies organically amended soils as compartments of particular interest and provides a baseline for targeted One Health surveillance of environmental AMR in tropical agroecosystems.

abstract: spp. are emerging foodborne pathogens posing public health risks through zoonotic transmission in agricultural settings. Characterizing their phylogenetic relatedness, antimicrobial resistance (AMR), and virulence factors is critical for assessing their impact on food safety and health in Ghana and Tanzania. We collected 144isolates (139 from farm animals and 5 from human clinical cases) and analyzed their genomes using molecular phylogenetics, antimicrobial resistance gene (ARG) profiling, and virulence gene identification. Extended spectrum beta lactamases and carbapenemase-producing Escherichia coli in humans, animals and the environment in East Africa: a scoping review
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is escalating in East Africa through close human-animal-environment interactions. Extended-spectrum beta-lactamases (ESBL) and carbapenemase-producingare clinically critical pathogens, yet local evidence is limited. This scoping review synthesizes evidence on ESBL and carbapenemase-producingin East Africa to inform One Health AMR control strategies. Following PRISMA-ScR guidelines, PubMed and Scopus were searched, identifying 279 records published between 2015 and 2025. After removing duplicates and screening, 185 articles were assessed for eligibility; 154 studies spanning human, animal and environmental sources met the inclusion criteria. Two reviewers independently extracted epidemiological, microbiological and molecular data in Covidence, including resistance genes and transmission evidence. The 154 included studies spanned 11 East African countries, led by Ethiopia ( = 55), Tanzania ( = 39) and Uganda ( = 22). Most studies (85.7%) were cross-sectional and human-focused (68.2%), with only 19 (12.3%) using a multi-sector One Health design. Overall, 21,554isolates were recovered from 74,700 samples. ESBL prevalence was reported in 117 studies (76.0%, median 46.8%) and carbapenemase prevalence in 65 (42.2%, median 3.3%), representing heterogeneous study-level estimates.predominated (89.9%), led by(26.1%); reported carbapenemase genes included,,andWhole-genome sequencing in 30 studies (19.5%) identified high-risk clones ST131, ST10, ST38 and ST410, though animal, food-chain and environmental sectors remained underrepresented. This review maps the current evidence on landscape for ESBL/carbapenemase- producingin East Africa, highlighting gaps in surveillance that are largely due to heterogeneity of available genomics data and limited longitudinal data within the "One Health" sectors. We recommend scaling up genomic capacity and standardized longitudinal surveillance to better understand national and regional AMR transmission and MDRinfections.

title: Dietary licorice improves carcass yield, hepatocellular protection, gut health, oxidative status, and cecal bacterial balance in broiler chickens
abstract: Over the past decade, phytotherapy such as licorice has attracted research as an alternative to antibiotic growth promoters in broiler production, driven by rising concerns over antimicrobial resistance. However, the consistency of its effects across productive, physiological, and health outcomes remains inconsistent. This meta-analysis quantitatively synthesized published experimental evidence on the effects of dietary licorice on growth performance, carcass yield, blood indices, visceral organs, oxidative status, intestinal morphology, and cecal bacterial balance in broiler chickens. A systematic literature search identified studies published between 2010 and 2025, and effect sizes were computed (Hedges'; 95% confidence interval). Pooled estimates were derived under the random-effects model using the restricted maximum likelihood estimator, with between-study heterogeneity characterized bythe-statistic. Univariable mixed-effects meta-regression was conducted to identify study-level moderators of treatment response, and publication bias was assessed using a funnel plot and the Rosenberg fail-safe N criterion. Dietary licorice did not affect feed intake or the feed conversion ratio, but it did increase body weight gain (BWG; SMD = 0.289; = 0.002), breast, thigh, gizzard, and bursa weights ( < 0.05). Gut integrity also improved with the villus height/crypt depth ratio (SMD = 0.931; = 0.041), andspp. counts (SMD = 0.266; = 0.003) increased, whilepopulations were suppressed (SMD = -1.737; < 0.001). Overall, the findings support that licorice enhances body weight gain, with route, duration, sex, and strain moderating efficacy.

abstract: ()is a globally pervasive and economically significant pathogen in bovine intramammary infections (IMIs) and is responsible for both clinical and subclinical mastitis. This study systematically investigated the global epidemiology offrom bovine IMIs, addressing antimicrobial resistance (AMR) amongthrough a meta-analysis. A total of 143 studies published between 2000 and 2025 were identified through comprehensive searches, which were based on predefined inclusion criteria. The data were systematically extracted, and the statistical analyses were performed in R (v4.5.2). The meta-analysis included 143 studies (145,457 samples), with a pooledprevalence of 24.78% and high heterogeneity (I = 99.51%). Subgroup analyses demonstrated significant heterogeneity in prevalence by study design, publication year, and region, with greater heterogeneity in cross-sectional studies (I>95%, < 0.001). Meta-regression identified sample size as a significant source of heterogeneity (β = -0.00002, = 0.02; R = 3.41%). The highest prevalence was reported in Cameroon (67%), Sri Lanka (64.3%), Indonesia (57%), and India (44%), with the lowest prevalence reported in Poland (0.7%), Taiwan (2.0%), Australia (5.5%), and New Zealand (5.3%). AMR was highest for doxycycline (70.7%), penicillin (65.2%), and ampicillin (62.8%); moderate to oxacillin (44.6%) and vancomycin (40.2%); and lowest for gentamicin (27.5%) and amikacin (18.3%). is highly prevalent in bovine IMIs worldwide, with marked regional heterogeneity and substantial resistance to commonly used antimicrobials, emphasizing the urgent need for targeted surveillance, prudent antimicrobial use, and improved mastitis control strategies at the global and regional levels.

N-acetylcysteine as an adjunct to antibiotics against bacterial biofilms: A systematic review of in vitro evidence
abstract: N-acetylcysteine (NAC) is investigated as an antibiotic adjunct, but acidity, formulation and experimental context complicate interpretation. We evaluated comparative in-vitro evidence while distinguishing biofilm prevention, established-biofilm treatment and resistance evolution. MEDLINE/PubMed, Embase, Scopus and Web of Science were searched through August 2026, with supplementary searching. Extraction distinguished NAC preparation and exposure pH, medium, hydrodynamics, NAC-alone controls, treatment intent and interaction methodology. Results were synthesized by experimental context, regimen, phase and endpoint without pooling or whole-study efficacy voting. Fifty-five studies were included: 7 evaluated combination exposure during formation only, 37 after establishment only, 9 both, and 2 resistance evolution. NAC-alone arms were documented in 39 studies, partial or formulation-specific in 9, and not identified in 7. Only two studies included a continuous-flow model. Selected combinations improved biofilm-associated outcomes, but intrinsic-acidic and neutralized preparations, biomass and viability endpoints, and planktonic versus biofilm interaction tests were not interchangeable. Liposomal and catheter-lock findings differed by dose matching, isolate and control set. Polymyxin findings varied with organism, resistance background, medium and exposure; rifampicin-alone and rifampicin-containing multidrug comparators addressed different questions. NAC is a context-dependent experimental adjunct, not an established class-wide antibiotic potentiator. The evidence does not support clinical antibiotic dose reduction or routine NAC combination therapy. Translation requires controlled final exposure pH, matched monotherapy and formulation controls, clinically relevant background regimens, viable-burden and regrowth outcomes, and resistance monitoring.

Combating antimicrobial resistance through multimodal data via artificial intelligence
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) poses a critical global health challenge, leading to substantial mortality and economic losses without science-based interventions. Conventional approaches to combating AMR have important limitations in addressing this escalating threat. Recent advances in AI, including deep learning, large language models, and protein language models, provide new opportunities to integrate multimodal data for AMR research. However, evidence remains uneven, with many approaches limited to computational benchmarking rather than real-world validation. Here, we critically review AI applications in AMR, focusing on rapid diagnosis, therapeutic discovery, and clinical decision support. AI-based diagnostic models can identify resistant pathogens and predict resistance profiles, but most lack prospective clinical evaluation. AI-assisted drug discovery and alternative therapies have generated promising candidates, although most remain at computational, in vitro, or early preclinical stages. Large language models may support decision-making, but their clinical use remains preliminary. Successful translation of AI into clinical and One Health practice will require representative datasets, independent validation, prospective evaluation, and robust governance.

Antimicrobial resistance patterns of bacteria isolated from milk samples of mastitic goats in Waghimra Zone, Amhara, Ethiopia
abstract: Mastitis is a multifactorial disease with major consequences for production, animal welfare, and public health, yet it remains less studied in goats than in cows. Moreover, reports of antimicrobial resistance among bacteria isolated from mastitic goats are scarce. In Ethiopia, treatment decisions for mastitis largely rely on empirical clinical experience rather than routine antimicrobial susceptibility testing. To address this gap, a cross-sectional study was conducted from November to December 2024 in Waghimra, Amhara, Ethiopia, to identify the major bacterial causes of mastitis and to evaluate their antimicrobial susceptibility patterns. Bacterial isolation, identification, and antimicrobial susceptibility testing followed standard protocols, and statistical analyses were performed using Stata 17 and WHONET software. The overall goat-level mastitis prevalence was 24.69% (98/397), comprising 2.52% (10/397) clinical and 22.28% (88/395) subclinical mastitis.spp. (47/129; 36.43%) was the predominant isolate, followed by(12/129; 9.30%) andspp. (3/129; 2.33%). Allisolates were resistant to ampicillin (37/37; 100%) and showed considerable resistance to tetracycline (16/37; 43.24%), but remained highly susceptible to kanamycin (36/37; 97.30%), chloramphenicol, and gentamicin (35/37; 94.59% each).andspp. were highly susceptible to most antimicrobials tested, except ampicillin. Multidrug resistance was detected in 13.46% (7 out of 52) of isolates, occurring exclusively amongspp. Subclinical mastitis, mainly caused byspp., was highly prevalent in the study area, showing complete ampicillin resistance and considerable tetracycline resistance. These findings have important implications for milk production, animal welfare, and public health, given local raw milk consumption.

Strengthening One Health Antimicrobial Resistance Surveillance in Bangladesh: Insights from the Fleming fund country grant
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is an escalating global public health concern, with particularly severe implications for low and middle-income countries such as Bangladesh. In Bangladesh context, fragmented surveillance systems and the extensive use of antimicrobials across human, animal, and aquaculture sectors contribute to the rapid emergence and spread of resistance. Strengthening integrated surveillance through a One Health approach is therefore crucial to support effective policy development and response strategies. This review outlines the policy, implementation, and key outcomes of the Fleming Fund Country Grant in Bangladesh between 2020 and 2025. It draws upon multiple data sources, including programme reports, routine AMR surveillance data, laboratory capacity-building initiatives, and stakeholder engagement activities across human, animal, aquaculture, and environmental sectors. Through this initiative, a coordinated national AMR surveillance network was established, comprising 20 laboratories across multiple sectors, including three designated national reference laboratories. The initiative strengthened surveillance through the introduction of standardized protocols and SOPs, improved diagnostic capacity, skilled workforce, and implementation of laboratory quality assurance systems, including EQA and NEQA. These measures enhanced the accuracy, consistency, and reliability of AMR surveillance data. In addition, the establishment of a national AMR data integration platform facilitated real time data sharing and evidence-based decision-making. A total of 208,346 bacterial isolates were analyzed, with AST results reported to the AMR dashboard across the human, and animal, health sectors. Overall, the Fleming Fund programme has made a substantial contribution to strengthening integrated AMR surveillance in Bangladesh by operationalizing a One Health framework. Continued political commitment, increased domestic investment, and the institutionalization of surveillance systems will be essential to sustain these gains and ensure long-term resilience against AMR.

Microfluidic-assembled curcumin ionizable lipid nanoparticles enhance aqueous delivery and antibiofilm activity against Staphylococcus aureus
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance and biofilm-associated infections demand novel therapeutic strategies. Curcumin is a natural polyphenol with broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity; however, its clinical utility is fundamentally constrained by negligible aqueous solubility and limited biofilm penetration. Here, we used microfluidic assembly to prepare curcumin-loaded ionizable lipid nanoparticles (Cur@LNP) with three clinically established ionizable lipids (SM-102, MC-3, and ALC-0315). The resulting formulations were uniform, with hydrodynamic diameters of approximately 90 nm and polydispersity indices near 0.1. Relative to free curcumin in DMSO, Cur@LNP lowered the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) 8-fold and the minimum bactericidal concentration (MBC) 16-fold against planktonic, and markedly reduced viable biofilm-resident cells at matched concentrations. Scanning electron microscopy showed that Cur@LNP treatment remodeled mature biofilms into irregular, debris-rich aggregates with reduced extracellular matrix coverage. Notably, antimicrobial performance was indistinguishable across the three structurally distinct ionizable lipids at every concentration tested. Within this in vitro, single-strain system, the antibiofilm effect is therefore dominated by the cargo (curcumin) rather than by ionizable-lipid chemistry, and it is most likely attributed to enhanced aqueous solubilization of curcumin rather than to engagement of the lipid headgroup with the biofilm matrix. These results position microfluidic-assembled ionizable LNPs as a reproducible, scalable solubilization platform for poorly water-soluble natural antimicrobials.

title: Metagenomic analysis of commensal small mammal samples from an international cargo shipping area, Bangkok Port, reveals potential zoonotic pathogens and implications for One Health surveillance
abstract: Commensal small mammals, such as rats and shrews, are recognized reservoirs for numerous zoonotic pathogens; however, their role in pathogen circulation at transport hubs remains underexplored. This study employs shotgun metagenomic sequencing to characterize microbial communities and assess zoonotic potential in tissue samples from commensal small mammals captured at Bangkok Port, an international cargo shipping hub in Thailand between June and August 2025. Following host read depletion, taxonomic profiling was performed to identify bacterial taxa of public health relevance, including sequences assigned tospp.,,, and. The virulence factor and antibiotic resistance gene profiles revealed that some of these pathogens have pathogenic potential and are related to drug-resistant bacteria. In addition,was identified as a shared taxon among rats, shrews, and their associated fleas. The findings support the ecological roles of mammalian hosts and their ectoparasites as reservoirs for pathogens of public health concern. These results emphasize the need to strengthen surveillance programs for commensal small mammals to monitor and mitigate the spread of transboundary pathogens at international maritime gateways.

Wild boar as a sentinel species for ecosystem health surveillance: A review
abstract: Sentinel surveillance uses selected species that are widely distributed, easily sampled, and exposed to multiple health threats as indicators of ecosystem health. The Eurasian wild boar () is a broadly distributed game species that meets these conditions. We conducted a systematic review to assess the suitability of the wild boar as a sentinel or indicator species for monitoring health hazards relevant to ecosystem health, focusing on the hazards monitored, methods, justification for use, perceived performance, limitations, and proposed improvements. We identified 86 studies explicitly framing the wild boar as a sentinel species, covering a wide range of hazards, including 30 pathogens, 44 environmental contaminants, two biological toxins and 13 antimicrobial resistance (AMR) indicators. It was used to monitor pathogens (57%), environmental contaminants (31.4%), AMR (12.8%), and biological toxins (3.5%). Research effort was concentrated in Europe (84.9%) and relied mostly on hunted animals (90.7%). Wild boar were frequently selected as sentinels due to their previous use as indicators of ecosystem health in the literature, omnivorous diet, wide distribution, and accessibility as game species. However, hunting-based sampling may introduce biases, while post-mortem conditions and ecological variability may affect results. Despite this, 74.4% of studies supported their use as sentinels, particularly for pathogens and environmental contaminants. In contrast, their perceived suitability for AMR was more variable, and no quality assessment was available for biological toxins. Overall, wild boar sentinel surveillance is considered logistically efficient and valuable for monitoring ecosystem health hazards. However, its effectiveness is context-dependent and influenced by methodological and ecological limitations. Improving surveillance design through systematic sampling, alternative sample sources (e.g., found-dead animals or non-invasive methods), integration of multi-species data, and inclusion of covariates could enhance the reliability of findings within a One Health framework.

title: Global spread of carbapenem-resistant Providencia driven by high-risk lineages and plasmid co-evolution
abstract: Carbapenem-resistant(CRP) is a formidable opportunistic pathogen with extensive drug resistance, posing an increasing threat to human, animal, and environmental health. However, its global genomic epidemiology and resistome-plasmidome co-evolution within a One Health context remain poorly understood. Here, we conducted a comprehensive population genomic and plasmid analysis of 1197 CRP isolates from 35 countries spanning 2012-2025. We reclassified the CRP population into ninespecies, identifyingandas established epidemic species alongside the rapid emergence ofand. We pinpointed 2019 as a critical inflection point, marking the transition from endemic stability to rapid global epidemic expansion (80.8% isolates in 2019-2025). Ten intercontinentally disseminated high-risk sequence types (e.g., ST46, ST79), each with strict species-ST specificity, were responsible for global spread. Thegene (62.4% prevalence) was the predominant carbapenem gene, exhibiting strong geographic and species specificity and mutual exclusion with other major carbapenem genes. Plasmids encoded approximately 80% of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) genes, with 78.0% of these plasmids belonging to 75 stable clusters. These clusters evolved a dual specialist-generalist strategy, with the broad-host-range cluster 72 mediating interspecies AMR transmission and cluster 7 acting as a super-vector carrying six carbapenem genes. Importantly, CRP circulated across interconnected human, animal, and environmental reservoirs, with distinct host-associated species distributions suggesting ecological niche adaptation and potential cross-host dissemination of resistance determinants. These findings demonstrate that the global expansion of CRP is driven by the combined evolution of high-risk clones and mobile genetic elements across interconnected ecological sectors, underscoring the need for integrated One Health surveillance and coordinated interventions spanning clinical, veterinary, agricultural, and environmental settings.

abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) has intensified in recent years, raising concerns about the potential impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on AMR dynamics. However, the influence of pandemic on the enviromental occurrence and dissemination of antibiotic-resistant genes (ARGs) remains under investigation. Wastewater-based epidemiology (WBE) provides an integrated view of community-level AMR dynamics, yet long-term assessments spanning the pandemic period remain limited. This study investigated the occurrence, temporal patterns, and seasonal behavior of two clinically relevant carbapenemase genes,and, in raw wastewater from the Attica region over a five-year period (July 2021-September 2025). A sensitive and specific 3-plex qPCR assay was developed and analytically validated for the simultaneous quantification of,, and 16S rRNA, the latter serving as a stable bacterial load indicator. Across the monitoring period,was consistently detected, showing a steady increase and reaching its highest concentrations in 2023, whileexhibited intermittent but pronounced surges, particularly in 2023. Comparison with community SARS-CoV-2 viral loads suggest temporal association with AMR signatures in wastewater. Seasonal analysis showed non-uniform patterns, with atypical warm-season peaks of both ARGs in 2023-2024 and a return to classical autumn-winter peaks in 2025, suggesting a gradual restoration of pre-pandemic seasonality. To our knowledge, this is among the first long-term WBE studies to characterize post-COVID-19 shifts in ARG occurrence and seasonality. The results demonstrate that the pandemic period was associated with elevated and fluctuating ARG levels in the urban wastewater system, emphasizing the need for sustained AMR monitoring. These findings address critical knowledge gaps in environmental AMR surveillance and support the integration of WBE into public health strategies aimed at mitigating AMR dissemination.

Genomic epidemiology to investigate the origins and zoonotic implications of antibiotic-resistant Escherichia coli on beef and lamb meat sold by independent butchers in Wales
abstract: Many studies have identified antibiotic resistant (ABR)on meat. Appropriate hand hygiene and cooking practices should minimize the risk of gastrointestinal colonisation with ABRfound on meat, and the subsequent chance of causing resistant opportunistic extraintestinal infection. There are large gaps in our understanding of the prevalence, origins and zoonotic potential of ABRfound on meat, however, and particularly for meat reared in extensive farming systems. Wales is a devolved nation within the United Kingdom having large populations of extensively-reared sheep and beef cattle. To help address knowledge gaps around ABRon extensively reared meat, therefore, beef mince and lamb loin/leg steaks/chops were purchased from 50 (beef) and 46 (lamb) independent butchers across Wales. Following enrichment culture, 200 g meat samples were found to be positive forresistant to amoxicillin (31% positivity), streptomycin (28%), spectinomycin (29%), amoxicillin-clavulanate (11%), 3rd generation cephalosporins (2%) and fluoroquinolones (5%). Phylogenetic analysis confirmed that Welsh lamb meat ABRisolates ( = 78) are more closely related to those found in faecal samples collected around sheep ( = 352) than around beef cattle ( = 361) on Welsh farms. This suggests that faecal contamination at or around slaughter is their primary origin. We found no closely related meat/infection clones (<20 SNPs distant and the same antibiotic resistance genes) when comparing ABRfrom Welsh meat ( = 91) and those causing extraintestinal infections in people ( = 2387) in an English region bordering Wales. We conclude, therefore, that the wider zoonotic implications of finding ABRon beef and lamb meat sold at independent butchers in Wales are small, though a more geographically and temporarily contemporaneous survey is warranted to address this further.

Sewage surveillance for assessing clinical antibiotic resistance prevalence: Combining metagenomic and phenotypic data
abstract: Surveillance of antibiotic resistance in clinical isolates is a cornerstone for the management of bacterial infections but is limited in large parts of the world, often due to lack of resources. Sewage surveillance has been proposed as a promising, resource-efficient complement to the traditional surveillance approach based on samples from many individual patients. Both phenotypic data on resistance in sewage isolates and abundance of antibiotic resistance genes in sewage have been shown to correlate with resistance prevalence in clinical isolates. Here, we aimed to directly compare and combine an isolate-based and a gene-based sewage surveillance approach to evaluate what best can reflect clinical resistance rates. The two approaches, based on susceptibility testing of collectedisolates and metagenomic sequencing, respectively, were applied to municipal sewage samples collected in ten European countries. The data generated was related to available data on resistance to aminopenicillins, fluoroquinolones, third generation cephalosporins and aminoglycosides prevalence in clinicalisolates using beta regression models. None of the tested individual predictors were superior across all four investigated classes of antibiotics. For modelling of aminopenicillin resistance, a clearly higher Rvalue was obtained when isolate-based and gene-based data was combined as predictors, also after adjusting for the number of included variables. We conclude that there could be a value of including both isolate- and gene-based sewage data for predictions of resistance rates in clinical isolates, while emphasizing the value of linking predictors to specific species and classes of antibiotics.

title: Clonal diversity, virulence factors and antibiotic resistance genes of Enterococcus faecalis and Klebsiella pneumoniae from urban rats in Malaysia
abstract: Peridomestic rats serve as important carriers of zoonotic pathogens, including multidrug-resistant bacteria such asand. However, information on the clonal diversity, antibiotic resistance, and virulence of these pathogens in wild urban rats remains limited, particularly in tropical settings. This study investigatedandin urban rats from wet markets across four Malaysian states. A total of 277 rats (, = 177;, = 100) were trapped, and lung tissues were processed for bacterial isolation. Isolates were identified by 16S rDNA sequencing and examined for antibiotic susceptibility, resistance genes, and virulence factors using PCR. Clonal relationships were determined through multilocus sequence typing (MLST). Nineteenand sevenisolates were recovered. Allisolates carried multiple virulence factors (,,, and), and four tetracycline-resistant isolates possessed,, and. Five novelsequence types (ST730 - ST734) were identified. Allisolates carried the SHV gene; two also harbored FOX, and two possessedandvirulence factors. Two novelSTs (ST2641 and ST2642) were detected. Phylogenetic analyses revealed that both species displayed diverse sequence types scattered across global lineages. These findings suggest that urban rats may act as potential carriers of virulent and antibiotic-resistantand. These findings support the inclusion of urban rats in future One Health surveillance programs investigating antimicrobial resistance and virulent bacterial pathogens.

abstract: Biofilm-associated infections caused by clinically important pathogens such as() and() remain a major challenge in healthcare settings due to enhanced antimicrobial resistance and persistence. In recent years, copper-coated carbon nanotubes (Cu-CNTs) have gained considerable attention as promising antimicrobial nanomaterials for preventing biofilm formation on medical devices and hospital-associated surfaces. This review summarizes recent advances in the development and application of Cu-CNT-based antimicrobial coatings, with an emphasis on their antibacterial and antibiofilm activities against Gram-positive and Gram-negative pathogens. The synergistic combination of the high surface-area-to-volume ratio of CNTs and the potent antimicrobial properties of copper (Cu) ions enhances microbial inhibition. Previous studies suggest that Cu-CNTs interfere with initial bacterial adhesion, inhibit biofilm maturation, and disrupt established biofilms through mechanisms involving oxidative stress generation, membrane destabilization, and cellular damage. Furthermore, the review discusses the physicochemical characteristics, antimicrobial mechanisms, biomedical applications, and potential challenges associated with Cu-CNT coatings, including toxicity and biocompatibility concerns. Overall, Cu-CNT-based coatings represent a promising strategy for developing durable antimicrobial surfaces to control chronic biofilm-associated infections and reduce healthcare-associated contamination.

Challenges and opportunities in antimicrobial R&D
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance is accelerating, while the discovery and development of new drugs, particularly those with novel mechanisms of action, have failed to keep pace. This widening gap reflects two major challenges: insufficient resources for antibiotic discovery and clinical development, and a lack of scientific innovation. With pharmaceutical companies largely abandoning antibiotic R&D, academic groups, small biotech companies, and not-for-profits are stepping in, harnessing advances in genomics, synthetic biology, and AI to drive discovery. Coupled with growing international investment and initiatives to address funding gaps, these efforts offer renewed hope for overcoming the antimicrobial resistance crisis.

title: Extracellular Polymeric Substances Govern Horizontal Gene Transfer of Antibiotic Resistance Genes: Mechanisms, Pathway Specificity, and Research Gaps
abstract: The dissemination of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) in environmental systems is recognized as being shaped by local matrix conditions, yet the pathway-specific role of extracellular polymeric substances (EPS), the dominant matrix of biofilms, sludge flocs, and granules, remains poorly resolved. In this Review, we develop a mechanism- and pathway-resolved perspective for evaluating how EPS govern horizontal gene transfer (HGT) of ARGs. Current evidence indicates that conjugation is the most directly supported pathway, with EPS facilitating or restricting transfer through effects on donor-recipient contact, matrix organization, and transfer-related physiology. For transformation, EPS-associated extracellular ARGs constitute reservoirs, but EPS-DNA binding can both preserve genetic material and limit its immediate bioavailability. By contrast, EPS involvement in phage-mediated transduction and vesicle-mediated transfer remains mechanistically plausible but insufficiently validated. We identify five interconnected mechanisms: physical retention and spatial organization, DNA adsorption and bioavailability, regulation of intercellular contact, modulation of cell physiology and transfer competence, and community-scale mobilome coupling. By clarifying evidence boundaries across pathways, this Review moves EPS-HGT research from correlation-based interpretation toward mechanism-informed assessment of ARG mobility. We conclude by outlining research needs, including standardized EPS definition and extraction, component-resolved characterization, pathway-resolved causal assays, and validation in realistic environmental aggregates.

title: Genomic analysis of Klebsiella pneumoniae bloodstream isolates reveals rare hypervirulence, no convergence with antimicrobial resistance, and a bla(SHV) promoter variant associated with elevated cefiderocol MICs at a German university hospital
abstract: Hypervirulent(hvKp) and the convergence of hypervirulence with antimicrobial resistance have raised concern worldwide, but contemporary, prospective data from Central Europe remain limited. We characterizedbloodstream isolates from a German university hospital, focusing on hypervirulence and antimicrobial resistance. Bloodstream isolates were collected at University Medical Center of Schleswig-Holstein, Lübeck, Germany, between May and December 2023. In total, 74were genotyped using whole-genome sequencing. Genomic virulence and resistance determinants were characterized with Kleborate and Russo criterion. A core-genome phylogeny was reconstructed. Hypervirulence was assessed genotypically and phenotypically using string test,growth kinetics, and thekilling assay. Findings were compared against 5,514 publicly available bloodstream-derived genomes. Genomically predicted hvKp were rare (2/74 by Kleborate; 1/74 by Russo) and belonged to the classical high-risk clones ST23 and ST380, neither of which carried acquired resistance genes. Eleven isolates were resistant to third-generation cephalosporins (nine, two), and two were carbapenem-resistant through. Three isolates carried a C-112Apromoter mutation associated with elevated cefiderocol MICs (0.5-4 mg/L). Neither growth kinetics norkilling distinguished the two hypervirulent isolates from non-hypervirulent. In the public data set, the overall hvKp prevalence was low, with no significant increase between 2012 and 2025. In this cohort, hypervirulentwas rare and showed no convergence with acquired resistance. These findings suggest that convergent MDR-hvKp lineages remain uncommon and support the continued use of genomic surveillance to detect their possible future emergence. Hypervirulent(hvKp) has emerged as a major public health concern because it causes more invasive and often more severe infections than classical, and its convergence with antimicrobial resistance could further limit treatment options. However, prospective data on the prevalence of hvKp specifically from bloodstream infections remain scarce, particularly in Europe. By combining genomic analysis of a prospective bloodstream-infection cohort with more than 5,500 publicly available genomes, we show that hypervirulent strains remain uncommon and that convergence with acquired antimicrobial resistance is still rare in this setting. These findings provide an important baseline for ongoing genomic surveillance of hvKp. In addition, the same surveillance approach also flagged a previously reportedpromoter variant associated with elevated cefiderocol MICs, indicating a potential emerging mechanism that warrants further investigation as cefiderocol use becomes more widespread.

title: Genomic profiling of Salmonella enterica subsp. enterica serovar Gallinarum strains isolated from ISA brown chickens (Gallus gallus domesticus) in Bangladesh
abstract: Non-typhoidal Salmonella serotypes cause most bird salmonellosis. We isolated and sequenced sixsubsp. enterica serovar Gallinarum strains from ISA Brown chickens. The genome size was ~4.7-4.9 Mb with ~52% GC content. Core virulence architecture essential for causing fowl typhoid, along with multidrug efflux pump-dependent antibiotic resistance, was detected.

title: Ecological Resilience and Microbial Dysbiosis in the Oral Microbiome: A Systems-Level Conceptual Framework
abstract: The human oral microbiome is a highly organised, dynamic microbial ecosystem that contributes to oral homeostasis through complex interactions among microorganisms, the host immune system and the local environment. Growing evidence indicates that oral diseases are associated with ecological disruption rather than the proliferation of individual pathogens alone. Environmental perturbations, including dietary changes, poor oral hygiene, smoking, antimicrobial exposure, ageing, salivary dysfunction and systemic disorders, can alter microbial community structure, functional activity and host responses, promoting dysbiosis. Established concepts, including the ecological plaque hypothesis, keystone pathogen hypothesis and polymicrobial synergy and dysbiosis model, explain complementary aspects of oral disease development. However, an integrated framework linking cumulative environmental stress, microbial interaction networks, ecological resilience, functional changes and host-microbiome feedback remains underdeveloped. This critical narrative review synthesises evidence from microbial ecology, multi-omics, systems biology, network analysis, antimicrobial resistance and oral-systemic interactions to propose the ecological collapse model (ECM) as a hypothesis-generating conceptual framework. The ECM proposes that oral dysbiosis may develop through interacting processes of functional adaptation, ecological destabilisation and persistent community disruption. The review also examines the oral microbiome as a reservoir of antimicrobial resistance determinants and discusses potential ecological interventions, including host-response modulation, precision antimicrobials and microbiome-directed therapies. These approaches may complement established oral healthcare but require further evaluation of their efficacy, safety and durability. The ECM provides a testable framework for investigating relationships among environmental perturbation, microbial function, ecological resilience and persistent dysbiosis. Longitudinal, experimental and translational studies are needed to determine whether its proposed indicators can predict disease progression or guide microbiome-informed interventions.

title: Long-term Changes in Pediatric Non-typhoidal Salmonella Epidemiology and Antimicrobial Resistance in Taiwan
abstract: Non-typhoidal Salmonella (NTS) remains a major cause of pediatric bacterial gastroenteritis. We investigated long-term changes in serogroup distribution and antimicrobial resistance (AMR) among pediatric NTS isolates in Taiwan. This retrospective surveillance study included children (<18 years) with culture-confirmed NTS gastroenteritis. Historical serogroup data were collected at Kaohsiung Veterans General Hospital during 1996-2002 and 2009-2015, and AMR patterns were compared with a contemporary cohort from Fu Jen Catholic University Hospital during 2024-2025. Susceptibility testing used disk diffusion for historical isolates and automated broth microdilution for contemporary isolates, with interpretation according to applicable Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute standards. Serogroup B declined from 72.3% (225/311) in 1996-2002 to 46.2% (399/864) in 2009-2015, whereas serogroup D increased from 8.4% (26/311) to 32.5% (281/864). Ampicillin resistance was 60.5% and 42.6% in the historical cohorts; among 4 contemporary isolates tested, 2 were resistant (50.0%, 2/4). Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole resistance decreased from 46.1% to 16.7% and then rose to 57.1% in the contemporary cohort. Resistance to ciprofloxacin and third-generation cephalosporins was detected in 28.6% and 14.3% of contemporary isolates, respectively; all 7 contemporary isolates were susceptible to cefepime, cefoperazone-sulbactam, imipenem and ertapenem. Pediatric NTS epidemiology in Taiwan changed substantially over 2 historical surveillance periods. Resistance to ciprofloxacin and third-generation cephalosporins was detected in the small contemporary comparison cohort, supporting continued culture-based surveillance, susceptibility-guided treatment, and antimicrobial stewardship.

title: Genomic and biological characterization of exopolysaccharides produced by Streptococcus thermophilus CCASU-ST-S3 and CCASU-ST-S52, with statistical optimization and preliminary spectroscopic characterization of EPS-STS3
abstract: Streptococcus thermophilus is a key dairy starter capable of producing exopolysaccharides (EPS) with strain-dependent biosynthetic and biological properties. Two EPS-producing strains, STS3 and STS52, isolated from yogurt, were characterized genomically, and their partially purified EPS preparations underwent preliminary biological evaluation. Whole-genome sequencing and bioinformatic analyses were used to confirm strain identity, assess safety-associated genomic features, and characterize EPS biosynthetic potential. Partially purified EPS preparations were evaluated for antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activities, cytotoxic effects, wound closure, and antimicrobial activity. EPS production by STS3 was optimized using one-factor-at-a-time screening followed by response surface methodology. The unoptimized EPS-STS3 preparation was separately subjected to preliminary spectroscopic characterization. Both strains contained Wzx/Wzy-dependent EPS biosynthetic loci with multiple glycosyltransferase- and Eps-associated genes; STS52 additionally carried a putative pel-like polysaccharide locus. Genome annotation identified nucleotide-sugar precursor pathways. Neither strain harbored acquired antibiotic resistance genes or virulence determinants. EPS-STS3 and EPS-STS52 preparations exhibited 2,2-diphenyl-1-picrylhydrazyl radical-scavenging activity (90.1% and 88.9%, respectively) and inhibited albumin denaturation. Both preparations produced dose-dependent reductions in cell viability, with greater effects in Caco-2 cells than WI-38 fibroblasts. The Caco-2 half-maximal inhibitory concentrations were 462.2 and 437.8 µg/mL, respectively. EPS-STS52 produced greater wound closure than EPS-STS3. EPS-STS3 produced promising antibacterial activity against tested Gram-negative bacteria; none was observed for EPS-STS52 or against Gram-positive bacteria or Candida. Optimization raised EPS-STS3 yield to 3.77 g/L (~ 23.56-fold above basal yield) under 3.8% sucrose, 5.8% peptone, pH 5.5, 47 °C, 32 h, and 3% inoculum. The optimized temperature exceeded that commonly reported for S. thermophilus EPS production. Ultraviolet analysis of EPS-STS3 showed no absorbance attributable to proteins or nucleic acids, while Fourier-transform infrared and ¹H/¹³C nuclear magnetic resonance data supported the carbohydrate nature. The two locally isolated S. thermophilus strains exhibited distinct EPS biosynthetic features, and their partially purified EPS preparations showed measurable biological activities under the tested conditions. EPS production by STS3 was substantially improved through statistical optimization, while preliminary spectroscopic characterization supported the carbohydrate nature of EPS-STS3. These findings support further structural characterization and biological evaluation of S. thermophilus-derived EPS using more specific and quantitative approaches.

Clinical, microbiological, and outcome profiles of liver abscess: a multicentre study in Bogotá, Colombia
abstract: Liver abscess remains associated with substantial morbidity and mortality, while data from Latin America are limited. This study aimed to describe the clinical characteristics, microbiological findings, antimicrobial resistance patterns, management strategies, and outcomes of liver abscess in tertiary-care centres in Colombia. We conducted a retrospective multicentre observational study including adult patients with confirmed pyogenic or amoebic liver abscess treated at four tertiary hospitals in Bogotá, Colombia, between 2015 and 2024. Demographic, clinical, imaging, microbiological, treatment, and outcome data were extracted from electronic medical records using a standardised REDCap form. 253 patients were included (median age 56 years; 64.4% male). Multiple abscesses were identified in 29.3% of patients (median 1 abscess per patient, IQR 1-2), with a median maximum diameter of 6 cm (interquartile range [IQR] 4-9). Abscess cultures were positive in 69.0% and blood cultures in 42.4%. Escherichia coli (34.5%) and Klebsiella spp. (28.3%) were the most frequently isolated pathogens. Extended-spectrum β-lactamase (ESBL) production, AmpC expression, and carbapenem resistance were detected, particularly among E. coli and Klebsiella spp. Percutaneous drainage was performed in 75.9% of patients. The median hospital stay was 12 days (IQR 7-20), 17.8% required intensive care unit admission, and in-hospital mortality was 5.3%. In this multicentre cohort of liver abscess patients from Colombia, pyogenic abscesses predominated, with a substantial burden of antimicrobial resistance among Enterobacterales. These findings emphasise the importance of local microbiological surveillance to guide empirical therapy and reinforce antimicrobial stewardship and early drainage strategies in middle-income settings.

title: Epicatechin Enhances Sulfamethoxazole Removal and Mitigates Representative Antibiotic Resistance Genes in a Bioelectrochemical System
abstract: The widespread occurrence of sulfamethoxazole (SMX) and antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) poses major challenges for wastewater treatment. This study evaluated purified epicatechin (EC), a representative tea polyphenol, as a natural electron mediator for simultaneous SMX removal and selected ARG mitigation in a bioelectrochemical system (BES). Compared with the no-EC control, EC addition improved SMX removal and reduced the relative and absolute abundances of the representative sulfonamide resistance genes and the class 1 integron integrase gene intI1. Compared with BES, the combined absolute abundances of these targets in BES-EC were 8.23-fold and 2.39-fold lower in carbon-felt biofilms and suspended sludge, respectively. EC promoted electroactive biofilms with greater redox capacity and pseudocapacitive current contribution, alongside a peak current density of 0.73 ± 0.03 mA m. These electrochemical improvements were accompanied by increased protein content in extracellular polymeric substances and enrichment of the fermentative genus Macellibacteroides and the electroactive genus Parazoarcus. Metagenomic and proteomic analyses revealed enrichment of functional genes and proteins associated with carbohydrate metabolism, electron transport, ATP synthesis, and the tricarboxylic acid cycle. These profiles were consistent with shifts in microbial carbon utilization and energy metabolism. EC-acclimated biofilms also maintained favorable SMX removal and bioelectrochemical performance after EC supplementation ceased. Together, these findings link improved SMX treatment and selected ARG mitigation to EC-associated changes in biofilm electrochemical properties and microbial functions. The results demonstrate the treatment potential of purified EC and provide a basis for evaluating polyphenol mediators recovered from tea waste.

title: Nano-selenium-engineered antibiotic delivery systems for acute bacterial meningitis: Therapeutic potential, evidence gaps, and translational challenges
abstract: Acute bacterial meningitis remains a life-threatening central nervous system infection associated with high morbidity and mortality worldwide, particularly in low- and middle-income regions. Despite the availability of broad-spectrum antibiotics, therapeutic outcomes are often compromised by poor drug penetration across the blood-brain barrier (BBB), suboptimal pharmacokinetics, and the growing prevalence of antimicrobial resistance. These limitations underscore the need for innovative drug delivery strategies capable of enhancing therapeutic efficacy while minimizing adverse effects. In this context, nanotechnology-based approaches have emerged as promising alternatives, with selenium nanoparticles (SeNPs) gaining increasing attention because of their distinctive physicochemical properties, intrinsic antimicrobial activity, antioxidant potential, and favorable biocompatibility. This review provides a critical evaluation of recent advances in nano‑selenium-based antibiotic delivery systems and their potential relevance to acute bacterial meningitis. Particular emphasis is placed on the multifunctional role of SeNPs as therapeutic agents and nanocarriers, including their potential to improve antibiotic stability, and stimuli-responsive drug release, and facilitate targeted delivery across biological barriers. The synergistic interactions between SeNPs and conventional antibiotics, including membrane disruption, and reactive oxygen species generation, are also examined. Importantly, although SeNP-based systems have demonstrated promising antimicrobial, antioxidant, and drug-delivery properties in various preclinical settings, direct disease-specific in vivo evidence demonstrating BBB transport and therapeutic efficacy in bacterial meningitis remains limited. Therefore, the potential application of nano‑selenium-based antibiotic delivery systems in bacterial meningitis should be considered an emerging research opportunity.

title: Can Regulatory Innovation Unlock the Full Potential of Phage Therapy Against Antimicrobial Resistance?
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is increasingly limiting the effectiveness of conventional antibacterial therapies, strengthening interest in bacteriophage therapy as a complementary and potentially personalized therapeutic approach. However, phage specificity, the need for adaptable cocktails, and the limited patentability of naturally occurring phages challenge regulatory pathways developed for standardized industrial medicines. This review examines the evolving regulatory landscape for therapeutic bacteriophages, focusing on the European Union and Italy. Recent developments, including European Pharmacopoeia General Chapters 5.31 (Phage therapy medicinal products) and 2.7.38 (Bacteriophage potency determination), the EMA's draft guideline on the quality aspects of phage therapy medicinal products, and the regulatory sandbox mechanism proposed by the EU, are progressively defining common standards for quality, manufacturing, and clinical development. National initiatives in Belgium, France, and Portugal illustrate complementary approaches to facilitating access to phage therapy, including hospital-based pharmaceutical production and compounding within regulated frameworks. Their legal scope and degree of implementation nevertheless differ substantially. Persistent challenges include limited controlled clinical evidence, fragmented access procedures, formulation and stability requirements, and insufficient investment incentives. Coordinated quality standards, systematic collection of clinical and pharmaceutical data, and specialized clinical-pharmaceutical networks could support the transition of phage therapy from exceptional access towards a more structured and evidence-based therapeutic option against AMR.

title: Effects of long-term polyethylene terephthalate microplastic exposure on anaerobic digestion: microbial community and antibiotic resistance dynamics
abstract: Microplastics are increasingly introduced into anaerobic digestion (AD) systems, yet their long-term effects on microbial succession and antibiotic resistance dynamics remain unclear. Here, a 120-day semicontinuous AD experiment investigated the effects of polyethylene terephthalate microplastics (PET-MPs) on digestion performance, microbial communities, antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs), mobile genetic elements (MGEs), and quorum sensing (QS)-related genes. By day 120, PET-MPs increased cumulative methane yield by 13% and enhanced volatile solids removal after an initial adaptation period. Microbial community succession was characterized by a shift from communities enriched in Bacillota and Bacteroidota toward those with higher relative abundances of Pseudomonadota and Actinomycetota. A total of 971 ARG subtypes and 649 MGE subtypes were detected. ARG and MGE richness decreased by 9.3-9.8% and 21.3-23.6%, respectively, during long-term operation, accompanied by increased evenness, while multidrug resistance became more prominent during late-stage operation. Microbial β-diversity was strongly correlated with ARG β-diversity (R = 0.95, p < 0.01) and MGE β-diversity (R = 0.93, p < 0.01). PET-MPs exposure was also associated with transient changes in QS-related genes and altered bacterial-ARG-QS associations. Overall, long-term PET-MPs exposure was associated with coordinated restructuring of microbial communities, ARGs, and MGEs, highlighting microbial community succession as an important ecological context for resistome and mobilome dynamics during prolonged microplastic exposure.

title: One Health priorities beyond 2026: translating advances in science, surveillance and governance into prevention and preparedness
abstract: The interdependence of human, animal and environmental health and persistent gaps between multisectoral commitments and effective implementation were highlighted in The Lancet 2023 One Health series. Since then, advances in genomic and environmental surveillance, artificial intelligence and international governance have created new opportunities for infectious disease prevention and preparedness. However, avian influenza A(H5N1), filovirus outbreaks, antimicrobial resistance and the 2026 Andes virus cruise-ship outbreak illustrate continuing challenges in surveillance, coordination and response. Climate-sensitive infections, foodborne zoonoses and environmental contamination further emphasize the need for integrated approaches extending beyond emerging viral threats. This review critically examines developments since 2023, distinguishing established preventive interventions from promising but incompletely validated technologies, and both proximate biosecurity controls and structural socio-ecological upstream prevention, from early detection and outbreak containment. We propose a six-stage surveillance-to-action pathway linking detection, verification, joint risk assessment, accountable decisions, coordinated interventions and double-loop evaluation. An operational matrix illustrates its application across emerging and endemic infections, antimicrobial resistance and environmental threats. Five priorities address interoperable participatory surveillance, evidence-based upstream prevention, integrated antimicrobial resistance action, sustainable national governance that redresses sectoral power asymmetries, and equitable regional capacity. Effective One Health implementation requires clear institutional responsibilities, sustained financing, co-designed community and indigenous participation and rigorous evaluation. Progress should ultimately be measured by demonstrable reductions in infectious disease risks and improved protection of human, animal and environmental health.

title: Genomic analysis of a novel phage species within a putative unassigned genus targeting ST11-KL64 carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae
abstract: Carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae (CRKP) is a critical pathogen threatening global public health. Phage therapy represents a promising alternative to antibiotics for treating CRKP infections. In this study, a novel phage belonging to a putative unassigned phage genus was characterized at the genomic level. Whole-genome sequencing was performed using an Illumina HiSeq X10 platform. Genomic features were analysed using various bioinformatics tools. Phage 150062 was isolated from fecal samples of free-range chickens raised on a smallholding in Sichuan Province, China, using a sequence type 11 (ST11) and K-locus type 64 (KL64) CRKP strain as the propagation host. The genome of phage 150062 is 111,827 bp in length, has 44.73% GC content, 150 coding sequences, and 4 tRNAs. Phage 150062 is putatively lytic, and no known virulence factor or antibiotic resistance genes were found through alignment with the Virulence Factor Database (VFDB) and the Comprehensive Antibiotic Resistance Database (CARD). Phage 150062 shares 88.13% overall genomic similarity with its closest relative phage sp. ELSA2. The evolutionary tree showed that phage 150062 exhibits the closest phylogenetic relatedness to phage sp. ELSA2. Collinearity analysis revealed genomic rearrangements and inversions between phage 150062 and its closest relative phage sp. ELSA2. Overall, phage 150062 represents a new species belonging to the same putative unassigned genus as phage sp. ELSA2. Phage 150062, which belongs to a novel species within the same putative unassigned genus as phage sp. ELSA2, expands the phage library targeting CRKP.

title: Bacterial neonatal conjunctivitis in a neonatal intensive care unit: incidence, aetiology, predictors, and antimicrobial resistance
abstract: To determine the incidence, aetiology, risk factors, and antimicrobial susceptibility profiles of pathogens associated with NC in a Brazilian NICU. This retrospective cohort study included neonates admitted to a NICU between January 2015 and June 2022. The research team conducted daily surveillance through systematic medical record reviews using standardized data collection forms and case definitions based on National Healthcare Safety Network criteria. Among 1,013 neonates, 12.3% developed bacterial conjunctivitis, with onset occurring at a median of 14 days of life (IQR: 9-19). Multivariable analysis identified prior peripherally inserted central catheter use and prolonged NICU stay as significant predictors of NC. Of the 140 bacterial isolates, 62.1% were Gram-positive bacteria (GPB), predominantly Staphylococcus epidermidis (43.7%), whereas 37.9% were Gram-negative bacteria (GNB), mainly Serratia marcescens (24.5%). Oxacillin resistance was detected in 64.6% of GPB, while multidrug resistance was identified in 5.7% of GNB. Ciprofloxacin eye drops showed high in vitro activity against the tested pathogens and were the most frequently used treatment. Neonates with conjunctivitis had a longer median hospital stay than those without conjunctivitis (30 vs. 9 days). Bacterial conjunctivitis was common among neonates admitted to the NICU and was predominantly associated with GPB, including oxacillin-resistant isolates. Ciprofloxacin showed high in vitro activity against the tested pathogens. Strengthening infection prevention and control measures and surveillance may help reduce the burden of neonatal conjunctivitis.

title: Co-exposure to bisphenol A and ofloxacin induces oxidative stress and energy metabolic dysfunction while altering mobile genetic element composition and enriching specific antibiotic resistance genes in Meretrix petechialis
abstract: Bisphenol A (BPA) and ofloxacin (OFL) are ubiquitous contaminants in aquatic environments and may pose combined risks to aquatic organisms. Although the toxic effects of BPA or OFL have been extensively investigated, the impacts of their co-exposure on intestinal health and antibiotic resistance in marine bivalves remain poorly understood. Therefore, this study employed Meretrix petechialis as a model organism and exposed it to BPA, OFL, and their combinations. The results indicated that co-exposure to BPA and OFL induced intestinal tissue damage and significantly enhanced oxidative stress. TEM observations and measurements of energy metabolism-related indicators revealed that co-exposure induced mitochondrial swelling and structural disruption, and reduced ATP content, NADcontent, and ATPase activity. Metagenomic analysis showed that co-exposure did not significantly alter the diversity and structure of the intestinal microbiota. However, the relative abundances of several multidrug, tetracycline, and fluoroquinolone resistance genes were significantly increased.
