Moreover, the hosts of most antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) remained stable, whereas several tetracycline resistance genes were detected in newly emerged carrier species. In addition, co-exposure altered the composition and species contribution patterns of mobile genetic elements (MGEs). Overall, this study demonstrates that co-exposure to BPA and OFL enhances oxidative stress in the intestinal tissue, perturbs energy metabolism, promotes the enrichment of specific ARGs, and alters the abundance of MGEs. These findings provide new insights into the ecological risks of combined BPA and antibiotic contamination in marine environments.

title: Worse Than Just the Sum of Its Parts: Polymicrobial Infection Demonstrates Synergistic Biofilm Formation and Bone Loss: A Murine Model of Periprosthetic Joint Infection
abstract: Periprosthetic joint infection (PJI) remains a leading cause of implant failure, with high treatment failure and mortality rates. Polymicrobial PJIs, particularly those involving Staphylococcus aureus (SA) and Candida albicans (CA), may be more common and difficult to eradicate than previously recognized. These coinfections are associated with enhanced biofilm formation, antimicrobial resistance, and worse clinical outcomes, but their in vivo impact remains poorly understood. We compared SA, CA, and SA + CA cocultures for biofilm formation on titanium, colony-forming units (CFUs), architecture as seen with scanning electron microscopy, and antimicrobial resistance. We then adapted a chronic murine PJI model in C57BL/6J mice to quantify longitudinal SA bioluminescence, end-point SA and CA CFUs, and femoral metadiaphyseal expansion by micro-computed tomography. CA coculture increased SA CFUs compared with SA monomicrobial infection and produced complex biofilm architecture on titanium. Co-biofilms showed increased resistance to vancomycin and amphotericin B. Coinfected mice had greater SA bioluminescence, 100-fold higher end-point implant CFUs of SA, and greater femoral metadiaphyseal expansion than mice with SA monomicrobial infection, without increased CA burden. Compared with SA monomicrobial infection, SA-CA coinfection enhanced SA biofilm formation, antimicrobial tolerance in vitro, and femoral remodeling in vivo, supporting a more severe bacterial-fungal periprosthetic joint infection phenotype. Polymicrobial PJI involving SA and CA may represent a distinct phenotype characterized by enhanced SA biofilm formation and femoral remodeling, supporting further study of improved diagnostics and targeted anti-biofilm strategies.

title: Characterization and heterologous expression of surface polysaccharides from pathogenic Enterococcus cecorum
abstract: Pathogenic variants of the chicken gastrointestinal bacteriumare of growing concern due to their ability to cause vertebral osteomyelitis, such as enterococcal spondylitis or "kinky back," when the bacteria infect the free thoracic vertebrae of broilers. Due to the elimination of prophylactic antibiotic feed treatment that was previously used to manage the disease, there is now a need to develop other strategies for preventing pathogenicinfections. In this work, we describe the structural characterization of two antigenic targets, a capsular polysaccharide and a rhamnopolysaccharide. Highly conserved biosynthetic gene clusters encoding enzymes for both structures have previously been identified in pathogenic. We show that these polysaccharides, when present on the surface of either the native or a heterologous host, induce an immune response in broilers. Furthermore, antibodies present in those sera cross-react with differentstrains and can induce killing of the pathogen in opsonophagocytosis assays. The characterization and heterologous expression of highly immunodominant cell wall polysaccharides that are conserved across many pathogenic strains is an important step toward the development of a potential glycoconjugate vaccine against.IMPORTANCEis a bacterium normally found in the gut of healthy chickens. However, pathogenic varieties ofexpressing surface capsular polysaccharides can cause skeletal deformations in the bird if the infection becomes systemic. This leads to severe morbidity and mortality in chickens raised for meat production and to significant financial losses for poultry producers. These infections were once managed by the inclusion of antibiotics in chicken feed; but this practice has been discontinued due to concern over antibiotic resistance development. We have identified polysaccharides that are conserved on the surface of many pathogenicthat induce protective cross-reactive immune responses in chickens when the polysaccharides are expressed on a benign bacterial carrier. As an alternative to antibiotics, this is an important first step toward the development of a vaccine that specifically targets many pathogenicisolates and may help to reduce financial losses while improving animal welfare.

title: Identifying phage host receptors using TraDIS
abstract: The growing antimicrobial resistance crisis has sparked renewed interest in using bacteriophage (phage) as a treatment for antibiotic-resistant infections. Phage are viruses that infect and often kill bacteria and have served as key models for many molecular biology studies. There are many complex phage-bacterial interactions that dictate the success or failure of the phage life cycle, but many of these are not well understood or characterized. These include the specific interactions to recognize a bacterium during the infection process, bacterial phage defense mechanisms, and metabolic pathways that are key to phage replication. In this study, a novelphage, Arnold, is characterized, and the genome sequence is reported. We then use transposon-directed insertion-site sequencing to screen a library ofmutants to identify over 200 genes involved in Arnold phage infection or in phage resistance. Using this approach, we identified both an outer membrane protein (BtuB, vitamin B12 transporter) and an inner membrane protein (SdaC, serine/proton symporter) that are essential for phage infection; deletions in these genes were shown to provide immunity to infection by this phage. Understanding the genetic basis of phage infection and phage resistance should allow us to select or design phage to target specific bacterial pathogens in the future. Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a global threat to modern health, and new solutions are needed to fight multi-drug resistant infections. One promising solution are bacteriophages, viruses that naturally infect and kill bacteria. Phage infection is very strain specific, governed by the interaction of phage proteins with a cell surface receptor. In order to understand the rules that govern which phage can infect which bacteria, we need to identify these interacting partners. We report the genome of a phage infectingand use transposon insertion sequencing to identify genes involved in phage infection, including what we propose are the cell surface receptors required for infection. This knowledge is essential for understanding and potentially engineering targeted phage treatments against specific bacterial pathogens.

title: 16S rRNA aminoglycoside resistance methyltransferases: an overview of structure, function, and fitness cost
abstract: SUMMARYAminoglycosides are important antibiotics used in the treatment of gram-negative and gram-positive bacterial infections; however, their clinical efficacy is increasingly compromised by the emergence of 16S rRNA methyltransferases. These enzymes confer high-level, broad-spectrum resistance to aminoglycosides by methylating the A site in 16S rRNA. The Arm family enzymes methylate G1405, conferring resistance to 4,6-disubstituted aminoglycosides. The Kam family enzymes methylate A1408, conferring pan-aminoglycoside resistance. Since their initial identification in clinical settings in the early 2000s, these enzymes have spread globally through mobile genetic elements, particularly within ESKAPE pathogens, frequently coexisting with carbapenemases to form extensively drug-resistant phenotypes. Structural studies show that both families possess a conserved Rossmann-fold architecture; however, they utilize different substrate recognition mechanisms, with clinical variants demonstrating increased catalytic flexibility relative to producer enzymes. The expression of these methyltransferases results in varying fitness costs depending on enzyme type, expression level, and disruption of housekeeping rRNA modifications. This review summarizes the current knowledge on the molecular mechanisms, global epidemiology, fitness effects, and new treatment options for resistance caused by 16S rRNA methyltransferases.

title: The mechanosensitive channel MscS links lipoteichoic acid synthesis alterations to beta-lactam sensitivity in Staphylococcus aureus
abstract: Lipoteichoic acid (LTA) is an essential cell envelope polymer inand contributes to beta-lactam resistance in methicillin-resistant(MRSA). Mutations that alter LTA synthesis sensitize MRSA to beta-lactam antibiotics, but the mechanism connecting the envelope polymer defects to antibiotic susceptibility has remained unclear. Here, using suppressor mutants with a mutation in RNA polymerase subunits, we found that LTA synthesis defects increased expression of a ParB-like protein and the mechanosensitive channel MscS. This locus was repressed in RNA polymerase suppressor mutants, which restored beta-lactam resistance, whereas induced expression of both genes reduced resistance. Increased ParBL-MscS expression was associated with decreased intracellular potassium and reduced cyclic di-AMP (c-di-AMP), linking altered membrane-envelope physiology to second messenger signaling. LTA synthesis mutants also showed reduced production of penicillin-binding protein 4 (PBP4), an important determinant of beta-lactam resistance. Modest restoration of PBP4 improved resistance in the mutant with reduced LTA abundance, whereas the mutant producing elongated LTA showed a distinct response, indicating that different LTA defects impose different envelope stresses. Also, under reduced LTA conditions, increased c-di-AMP level alone was not sufficient to restore PBP4 expression and beta-lactam resistance. Together, these findings identify a potassium-dependent pathway connecting LTA synthesis, mechanosensitive channel activity, c-di-AMP signaling, PBP4 production, and beta-lactam resistance. This work reveals how cell envelope perturbations are converted into cytoplasmic regulatory responses that control antibiotic susceptibility and suggests that ion homeostasis and c-di-AMP signaling may be exploitable pathways for restoring beta-lactam efficacy against MRSA.IMPORTANCEAntibiotic-resistant, including methicillin-resistant(MRSA), is difficult to treat because it can withstand many beta-lactam antibiotics. Changes in lipoteichoic acid (LTA), a major cell-envelope polymer, increase beta-lactam sensitivity, but the underlying mechanism has been unclear. Here, we show that LTA synthesis defects activate a pathway involving the predicted membrane channel MscS. This pathway lowers intracellular potassium, reduces cyclic di-AMP signaling, and decreases production of PBP4, a cell-wall synthesis enzyme that contributes to beta-lactam resistance. These changes make MRSA more vulnerable to beta-lactam antibiotics. Our findings show that antibiotic resistance depends not only on drug targets but also on coordination between the cell envelope, ion homeostasis, and intracellular signaling. This connection identifies physiological pathways that may be exploited to restore beta-lactam efficacy against resistant.

title: Prevalence of Antibiotic Allergy in Patients with Inborn Errors of Immunity
abstract: Patients with inborn errors of immunity (IEI) are frequently exposed to antibiotics due to increased susceptibility to infection. Published data regarding rates of medication allergy in IEI are conflicting and may report higher rates of antibiotic allergy compared to the general population. However, many reported antibiotic allergies are not formally evaluated, leading to unnecessary avoidance of first-line antimicrobial therapy. Accurate identification of true antibiotic allergy is therefore important, as inappropriate allergy labels may contribute to the use of broader-spectrum antibiotics, increased antimicrobial resistance, higher healthcare costs, and suboptimal patient outcomes. This study will be conducted at Westmead Hospital, where patients with confirmed IEI currently receiving immunoglobulin replacement therapy will be reviewed to identify documented medication allergy labels, including implicated medications, reaction characteristics, and results of antibiotic testing performed. Results will be described, and statistical analysis will be used to determine the prevalence and characteristics of medication allergy in this population. The findings of this project will help determine the prevalence of medication allergy within our cohort of patients and contribute to the currently limited body of knowledge regarding medication allergy in patients with IEI. The results may also help identify the need for larger collaborative studies involving other immunology units and support future research into antibiotic allergy assessment and de-labelling strategies aimed at improving antimicrobial stewardship and expanding safe treatment options for this patient population.

title: Valnemulin, a repurposed oral drug, demonstrates dual activity against Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis
abstract: The most prevalent bacterial sexually transmitted infections are caused byand. According to the World Health Organization, over 211 million cases were reported in 2020. Currently, ceftriaxone is the only recommended single-dose intramuscular therapy for gonorrhea, but it exhibits minimal to no efficacy against chlamydial infections. Azithromycin and doxycycline are recommended to treatinfections; however,has developed resistance to both. Hence, no single drug is available that can effectively target both pathogens. Through a drug repurposing approach, with a particular focus on uncommon or underexplored drugs, we identified valnemulin, a pleuromutilin derivative and veterinary antibiotic, as a potent dual-acting agent. Valnemulin showed potent activity against multidrug-resistant, with its minimum inhibitory concentrations as low as 0.03 μg/mL and retained activity against azithromycin-resistant. Additionally, valnemulin demonstrated anti-.activity at concentrations of 0.008 μg/mL. Moreover, valnemulin exhibited rapid bactericidal activity, a prolonged post-antibiotic effect, and a low propensity for resistance development. Insights into the mechanisms of action and binding sites were investigated as well. Valnemulin exhibited potent inhibition in the bacterial transcription/translation assay with an ICvalue of 0.07 μg/mL. Molecular docking with the 23S rRNA crystal structure revealed a highly favorable interaction with a binding affinity of -9.197 kcal mol. In a murine genital tractinfection model, a single day of valnemulin treatment reduced gonococcal burden by 83%. Overall, our findings demonstrate that valnemulin is a promising candidate to treat sexually transmitted infections and deserves further investigation. The traditional drug discovery process is both time-consuming and costly, typically requiring 10-15 years and costing around $2 billion. Therefore, a therapeutic repurposing approach has emerged as an efficient alternative strategy for drug discovery that significantly reduces development time and cost. In an effort to identify new therapeutics against/infections through a drug repurposing approach, valnemulin was identified as a promising anti-and anti-agent.

title: Effects of memantine on the in vitro activity of antibacterial and antifungal agents against resistant bacterial and fungal pathogens
abstract: Patients on long-term memantine therapy often require antimicrobial treatment, yet susceptibility testing omits this co-administered drug. This study evaluated whether memantine alters theactivity of antimicrobial agents against resistant clinical pathogens. Seven reference strains and 140 resistant or non-wild-type clinical isolates of,,,,,andwere tested by broth microdilution to determine minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs). Interactions were assessed by checkerboard assay and confirmed by 24 h time-kill analysis in triplicate. Memantine reduced the partner antimicrobial MIC in all 147 strain-drug combinations. Fractional inhibitory concentration index (FICI)-defined synergy (≤0.5) was identified in 23 isolates spanning all seven pathogen groups, including carbapenem-resistantand azole-resistant; the remainder showed no interaction (FICI >0.5-4.0), with no antagonism. Time-kill analysis confirmed synergy in all 23, with reductions of 4.54-6.93 logcolony-forming units (CFU)/mL at 24 h without regrowth. Seven isolates with comparable MIC reductions but FICI above 0.5 showed no additional killing. Memantine modulates antimicrobial activityacross a broad panel of resistant pathogens. The concentrations involved exceed therapeutic plasma levels and identify drug-organism pairs warranting pharmacokinetic-pharmacodynamic and mechanistic investigation.

title: Multimetallic SPIONs disrupt cellular homeostasis in Mycobacterium tuberculosis
abstract: The development of new approaches to combat(Mtb) remains important, because antimicrobial resistance continues to complicate tuberculosis treatment. Metal-based nanomaterials offer one avenue for investigation, particularly when combined with existing bioactive compounds. This study evaluated the antimycobacterial activity of metal-coated superparamagnetic iron oxide nanoparticles (SPIONs) against virulent Mtb H37Rv and investigated their potential to enhance the activity of repurposed drugs. Silver-coated SPIONs (Ag@SPIONs), Cu-coated SPIONs (Cu@SPIONs), and silver-copper‑coated SPIONs (Ag-Cu@SPIONs) were synthesized and loaded with sulfadiazine and meloxicam. Antimycobacterial activity was assessed using minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) and growth inhibition kinetic assays, while ultrastructural changes were examined by scanning electron microscopy. RNA sequencing was performed to characterize Mtb transcriptional responses to nanoparticle exposure. Ag-Cu@SPIONs exhibited the greatest activity among the unloaded nanoparticles (MIC = 31.25 µg/mL). Drug-loading enhanced antimycobacterial activity, with sulfadiazine-loaded Ag@SPIONs showing the highest activity (MIC = 7.8 µg/mL). Nanoparticle exposure caused cell-envelope damage and disruption of cellular integrity. Transcriptomic analysis revealed perturbations in genes associated with cell-envelope maintenance, energy metabolism, oxidative-stress responses, and cellular homeostasis, with Ag-Cu@SPIONs producing the most pronounced transcriptional changes. Metal-coated SPIONs exhibited antimycobacterial activity against Mtb H37Rv, while drug-loading further enhanced their efficacy. These findings support hybrid nanomaterials as promising candidates for developing alternative antimycobacterial strategies.

title: Genome-to-Image Translation: Reconstructing Escherichia coli Morphology from Genomic Sequences
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance in Escherichia coli is established in routine practice by culture-based susceptibility testing, which is slow relative to the clinical need for an early treatment decision. Resistance status also leaves a measurable trace in cell morphology, and whole-genome sequencing of clinical isolates is increasingly available, which raises the question of whether colony appearance can be predicted directly from an isolate's genome. We formulate this as a conditional image-generation problem. The assembled contigs of each isolate are encoded into a single 768-dimensional vector by a frozen genomic language model through a segment-contig-isolate aggregation hierarchy, and a conditional Wasserstein GAN with gradient penalty synthesizes colony images from this embedding together with the applied antibiotic and the resistance label. We train on 167,356 single-cell images from 22 clinical blood isolates imaged under azithromycin, ciprofloxacin, tetracycline, and a no-drug control, compare seven pretrained convolutional backbones inside the generator, and select ConvNeXt-Tiny on distributional image-quality metrics. The synthetic images are then assessed extrinsically: added to a reduced real training set, they improve per-antibiotic resistance classification, with a significant gain in resistant-class recall.

title: Bimetallic Sites Cu/Co Alloy Targeting Quorum Sensing Reversing MRSA Ciprofloxacin Susceptibility
abstract: The escalating global prevalence of infections caused by resistant pathogens emerge as a critical public health crisis, especially in implants. It underscores urgent imperative to advance novel and efficacious strategies combating antimicrobial resistance. Herein, Cu-bearing cobalt-based (CoCrMo-Cu) alloys with bimetallic active sites (Cu/Co) are designed to effectively restore methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) sensitivity to ciprofloxacin, the most representative resistant antibiotic against MRSA. By combining CoCrMo-Cu with ciprofloxacin, proposing a synergistic dual-action platform addressing MRSA-infected osteomyelitis. Results show that CoCrMo-Cu exhibit anti-infection through two-stage process: disrupting biofilm, the extrinsic physical resistance barrier. Specifically, real-time bacterial motility trajectories reveal CoCrMo-Cu disrupt bacterial initial exploration behaviors, inhibiting biofilm development. Second, inhibiting intrinsic resistance barrier: efflux systems, enhancing effectiveness of antibiotics. Such comprehensive anti-infective mechanism is attributed to quorum quenching through satisfactory reactive oxygen species generation from bimetallic active sites. Eventually, MRSA resistance to ciprofloxacin is reversed and it results in an 87.5% reduction of minimum inhibitory concentration for ciprofloxacin. CoCrMo-Cu combining with ciprofloxacin significantly eradicates MRSA-infected osteomyelitis in vivo. Unlike stop-gap solutions focus on developing novel antibiotics, we prioritize restoring MRSA susceptibility to conventional antibiotics, providing a long-term strategy addressing resistant bacterial infection with enhanced sustainability.

title: Integrating algal-bacterial consortia and Daphnia magna cultivation for aquaculture wastewater treatment: Water polishing, pathogen control, and live feed production
abstract: Recirculating aquaculture systems face bottlenecks in energy-efficient wastewater polishing, cost-effective biomass harvesting, and high-value resource recovery. This study developed an integrated ecological treatment chain coupling light-driven algal-bacterial consortia with Daphnia magna cultivation for aquaculture wastewater treatment and reuse. Three photobioreactors were established with different initial microbial species to cultivate consortia directly from artificially-simulated aquaculture wastewater: C. vulgaris alone (R1), C. vulgaris plus M. pulcherrima (R2), and C. vulgaris plus B. subtilis (R3). After 100-day operation, all reactors achieved effluent quality compliant with recirculating aquaculture systems water reuse standards. Among them, R2 exhibited the most favorable performance: superior early-stage ammonia removal (effluent NH-N < 0.5 mg/L), the largest floc size (179.83 μm), the lowest pathogenic Arcobacter abundance (< 0.01 %), and significantly reduced relative abundances of certain antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs). When photobioreactor effluents were used as culture media for D. magna, R2 effluent supported the highest ingestion rate (1.2 ± 0.1 × 10cells·ind·h) and a 21-day survival rate of 88.9 ± 2.6 %, exceeding the conventional yeast feed control (79.6 ± 1.3 %). Metabolomic analysis revealed 821 differential metabolites in R2-cultured D. magna (595 upregulated), with significant enrichment in eicosapentaenoic acid, functional amino acids, vitamins, and cofactors. These results demonstrate that the algal-bacterial consortium-D. magna coupling enables simultaneous wastewater polishing, pathogen suppression, ARGs risk mitigation, and high-value live feed production, providing a sustainable approach for aquaculture wastewater treatment and live feed production.

title: International Nosocomial Infection Control Consortium (INICC) report of healthcare-associated infections, data summary of 44 countries for 2017-2022, Adult and Pediatric Units, Device-associated Module
abstract: We report International Nosocomial Infection Control Consortium (INICC) data from 2017 to 2022 on 499 intensive care units (ICUs) in 44 countries across Asia, Eastern Europe, Latin America, and the Middle East. Prospective ICU patient data were collected via the INICC Surveillance Online System. CDC/NHSN definitions were applied to device-associated healthcare-associated infections (DA-HAIs). We collected data on 274,653 patients, 1,685,152 patient-days, 794,473 central line (CL)-days, 576,956 mechanical ventilator (MV)-days, and 1,024,993 urinary catheter (UC)-days. We identified 3,001 CL-associated bloodstream infections (CLABSI), 4,623 ventilator-associated pneumonias (VAP), and 2,829 UC-associated urinary tract infections (CAUTI). Combined DA-HAI rates were 3.81 per 100 patients and 6.20 per 1,000 patient-days. CLABSI occurred at 3.78 per 1,000 CL-days, VAP at 8.01 per 1,000 MV-days, and CAUTI at 2.76 per 1,000 UC-days. Resistance reached 72.9% to ceftriaxone and 58.6% to imipenem in Klebsiella pneumoniae; 75.8% to cefotaxime in Escherichia coli; 42.9% to ceftazidime and 55.1% to imipenem in Pseudomonas aeruginosa; and 88.3% to piperacillin-tazobactam and 88.5% to imipenem in Acinetobacter spp. Methicillin resistance in Staphylococcus aureus was 45.3% and vancomycin resistance in Enterococcus faecalis 8.0%. DA-HAI rates were 2.1 to 7.3 times CDC/NHSN pooled means, and bacterial resistance was high, supporting continued prevention.

title: Towards Edge Artificial Intelligence for Predicting Antimicrobial Resistance in Mycobacterium tuberculosis
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MTB) poses a major challenge to global tuberculosis control, as multidrug-resistant strains limit available treatment options. Rapid and accurate prediction of drug resistance from genomic data could support timely treatment decisions and public health interventions. However, many existing computational approaches for genomic AMR prediction rely on computationally intensive pipelines, limiting their suitability for deployment on resource-constrained edge devices. This limitation is particularly relevant in hospital settings in low- and middle-income countries, where computing infrastructure and access to high-performance computational resources may be limited. To address this challenge, we present a lightweight, novel machine learning (ML) approach suitable for running on edge devices that combines 4-mer frequency features derived from whole-genome sequences with a Random Forest classifier to predict antibiotic resistance in MTB. The proposed ML approach achieved an average area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.82 across 20 antibiotics on an independent test set.

title: MaldiSuite: a Python ecosystem for MALDI-TOF spectral processing and analysis in antimicrobial resistance research
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a major global health threat requiring faster diagnostics than the 24-48 h needed for phenotypic antibiotic-susceptibility testing. Matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization time-of-flight (MALDI-TOF) mass spectrometry is widely used in clinical microbiology for species identification but does not directly capture AMR phenotypes. Machine learning on MALDI-TOF spectra offers a promising solution, yet existing software remains fragmented across legacy R preprocessing tools and ad hoc Python scripts, lacking standardized workflows, shared application programming interfaces (APIs), and safeguards against train-test leakage. We present MaldiSuite, a unified Python ecosystem built on a shared data model and a scikit-learn-compatible API. It integrates three packages: MaldiAMRKit (Bruker-native and open-format input/output, standardized composable preprocessing, spectral warping, and temporal drift monitoring); MaldiBatchKit (multi-site batch correction, including MALDI-specific methods, with batch-mixing diagnostics); and MaldiDeepKit (four deep-learning classifiers: multilayer perceptron, one-dimensional convolutional neural network, residual network, and Vision Transformer). All components compose within sklearn.pipeline.Pipeline with leak-safe fit/transform semantics. On the public multi-site Database of Resistance Information on Antimicrobials and MALDI-TOF Mass Spectra (DRIAMS), MaldiSuite achieves an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of up to 0.92 on the DRIAMS-A Staphylococcus aureus/oxacillin task, and a leakage experiment quantifies the optimistic bias that its leak-safe cross-validation removes. MaldiSuite is available on PyPI under the MIT licence (pip install maldisuite). Source code: https://github.com/EttoreRocchi/MaldiSuite, https://github.com/EttoreRocchi/MaldiAMRKit, https://github.com/EttoreRocchi/MaldiBatchKit, https://github.com/EttoreRocchi/MaldiDeepKit. The package versions described here and the analysis code of this paper (https://github.com/EttoreRocchi/MaldiSuite-paper), with the pinned environments, are archived at 10.5281/zenodo.24199316. https://ettorerocchi.github.io/MaldiSuite/. Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.

title: Stepwise phage isolation effectively suppresses Salmonella Gallinarum and facilitates the potential discovery of novel phage species
abstract: Salmonella enterica serovar Gallinarum, the causative agent of fowl typhoid, remains a major threat to poultry production due to high mortality and increasing antimicrobial resistance. Although bacteriophages are promising antibacterial agents, their application is frequently limited by rapid emergence of phage-resistant bacterial populations, leading to bacterial regrowth. Strategies that consider phage-resistant bacterial regrowth during phage selection may improve cocktail design; however, such approaches have not been systematically explored in S. Gallinarum. Here, we applied a phage-resistant-host-based stepwise isolation strategy to develop a phage cocktail targeting S. Gallinarum. An initial lytic phage (S8) was isolated, and phage-resistant mutants generated during treatment were subsequently used to isolate two additional phages (C2 and Th1). The three phages represented distinct morphotypes and genera. In vitro assays showed that the three-phage cocktail, applied at an MOI of 1, suppressed bacterial growth for 24 h, with ODreadings remaining below the detection limit, and reduced phage-insensitive bacterial regrowth compared with single-phage treatments. Genomic screening identified no virulence- or antibiotic resistance-associated genes, while BACPHLIP analysis predicted virulent lifestyles for all three phages. VIRIDIC analysis further supported the distinct species-level classification of C2 within the genus Teseptimavirus. These findings suggest that the phage-resistant-host-based stepwise isolation enables rational phage cocktail design to improve bacterial suppression and mitigate resistance-driven regrowth in S. Gallinarum.

title: Which rapid susceptibility testing methods for new antibiotics in clinical practice? a narrative review
abstract: Multidrug-resistant Gram-negative bacteria are among the leading contributors to antimicrobial resistance-associated morbidity and mortality worldwide, underscoring the need for prompt and effective antimicrobial therapy. Novel β-lactam/β-lactamase inhibitor (BL/BLI) combinations and cefiderocol have expanded therapeutic options against carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales, Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Acinetobacter baumannii. However, conventional antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST) methods remain slow, resistance to these newer agents is emerging, and delayed results may prolong empirical broad-spectrum or inappropriate therapy. To summarize available rapid AST methods for novel anti-Gram-negative antibiotics, with a focus on analytical performances, practical limitations and laboratory implementation. Narrative review of the literature on molecular and phenotypic rapid AST methods, including rapid disc diffusion method, AST platforms, and colorimetric assays applied to novel BL/BLI combinations and cefiderocol. Relevant literature was identified through non-systematic searches of PubMed/MEDLINE and Embase conducted between January 2022 and May 2026. Molecular assays allow rapid detection of resistance genes but remain complementary to phenotypic AST methods, owing to incomplete coverage of resistance mechanisms and imperfect genotype-phenotype correlation. Rapid disc diffusion and automated AST methods shorten time to results (TTR) and enable earlier phenotypic categorization, while innovative AST platforms can provide accurate minimum inhibitory concentrations. Rapid, low-cost colorimetric assays, not yet commercialised, can detect resistant isolates regardless of the underlying mechanism. However, only a few novel BL/BLI combinations are covered by these methods, and their performances depend strongly on the resistance mechanism. Cefiderocol testing is particularly challenging, as reliable susceptibility determination requires iron-depleted conditions, which limits rapid testing. Clinical outcome data remain scarce. Rapid AST methods for novel antibiotics is advancing and can reduce TTR, but gaps persist in performances, antibiotic coverage and evidence of clinical impact. Integration into optimized laboratory workflows and antimicrobial stewardship programmes is essential to translate faster results into improved prescribing and patient outcomes.

title: Age- and sex-related differences in Staphylococcus epidermidis and Corynebacterium spp. on the adult ocular surface
abstract: Ocular surface bacterial flora is a potential source of bacterial keratitis and post-operative endophthalmitis, but age- and sex-related differences in ocular surface bacterial flora and antimicrobial resistance remain unclear. We investigated these differences in bacterial isolates and levofloxacin (LVFX) susceptibility in adults. Retrospective study. We reviewed microbiological data on conjunctival isolates from 18,053 eyes of 11,677 adults without ocular infection undergoing ophthalmic surgery at the Miyata Eye Hospital between June 2018 and December 2023. Data were analyzed using generalized additive and log-linear model. LVFX susceptibility was determined using the Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute broth microdilution protocol. 22,561 bacterial isolates (11,081 from women; 11480 from men) were obtained from adults aged >19 years. The number of species isolated from women was lower than men, and increased at a rate of 1.19 and 1.09 per 10 years of age in women and men, respectively (p < 0.0001). Staphylococcus epidermidis and Corynebacterium spp. were predominant across all age groups. Under 80 years of age, methicillin-sensitive S. epidermidis (MSSE) was isolated more frequently from men than from women. Corynebacterium spp. increased with age in both sexes. Between age 40-90 years, LVFX resistance in MSSE was higher in women than in men, whereas LVFX resistance in Corynebacterium spp. increased with age regardless of sex. S. epidermidis and Corynebacterium spp. showed age- and sex-related differences in isolation frequency and fluoroquinolone susceptibility. Age and sex may influence ocular surface microbial ecology, antimicrobial resistance, and perioperative infection control.

title: Metal-1,10-phenanthroline-5,6-dione complexes target multidrug-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii: antibacterial and pharmacodynamic insights
abstract: The escalating threat of antimicrobial resistance underscores the need for novel therapeutic strategies against multidrug-resistant (MDR) Gram-negative pathogens. In this context, we previously demonstrated the potent antimicrobial activity of 1,10-phenanthroline-5,6-dione (phendione) complexes with silver(I) [Ag(phendione)₂]ClO₄ (Ag-phendione) and copper(II) [Cu(phendione)](ClO)·4HO (Cu-phendione) against Acinetobacter baumannii. Herein, we further characterized their antibacterial and pharmacodynamic profiles against six MDR clinical isolates of A. baumannii and the reference strain ATCC 19​606. Exposure-response relationships, dose-fractionation regimens, post-antibiotic effects (PAEs), inoculum effects, carbapenem interactions, and bacterial tolerance, persistence and heteroresistance were investigated. Ag-phendione exhibited bactericidal activity against all seven strains at 16× MIC between 6 and 12 h, whereas Cu-phendione showed strain-dependent bactericidal or bacteriostatic effects. Exposure-response and dose-fractionation analyses suggested that exposure timing influenced antibacterial activity, although concentration also contributed to bacterial killing. Two doses of 0.5× MIC administered 6-h apart resulted in counts below the detection limit in 12 of 14 compound-strain conditions within 24 h. Inoculum assays showed that 3.125 µg/mL inhibited growth in 69 of 70 (98.6%) conditions. Ag-phendione produced a longer mean PAE than Cu-phendione (1.857 ± 0.378 versus 0.714 ± 0.488 h; p = 0.0156). Checkerboard assays showed predominantly additive interactions with meropenem and imipenem, whereas time-kill assays identified synergy in two of 14 meropenem-compound combinations. TDtest showed no reproducible pattern characteristic of tolerance or heteroresistance within the scope of the assay. These findings provide a foundation for further investigation of phendione-based complexes, particularly to assess their activity under physiologically relevant conditions and establish their safety and in vivo efficacy.

title: 4-imidazolecarboxaldehyde attenuates virulence and pathogenicity of Pseudomonas aeruginosa by targeting las and rhl systems
abstract: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is an important pathogen which often causes serious and difficult-to-treat infections in humans due to its high intrinsic and acquired antibiotic resistance, highlighting an urgent need for novel therapeutic strategies or agents. QS system serves as the core regulatory network governing virulence and antibiotic resistance of PA, has been recognized as important targets for anti-virulence therapy. In this study, 4-Imidazolecarboxaldehyde, a 4-formyl imidazole derivative, was identified as a promising QS inhibitor that could significantly suppress the expression of the QS-associated genes of lasI/R, rhlI/R, pqsA/R, lasA, rhlA and phzA1, and inhibit the corresponding virulence factor production of lasA encoded protease, rhlA related rhamnolipid and phzA1 associated pyocyanin, as well as the motility and biofilm formation in Pseudomonas aeruginosa PAO1 at sub-MICs of 80 and 160 µg/mL. The pathogenicity of PAO1 could also be attenuated by 4-imidazolecarboxaldehyde at 80 and 160 µg/mL, verified by Chinese cabbage, D. melanogaster and C. elegans infection analysis. 4-Imidazolecarboxaldehyde might target las and rhl systems to interfere with QS system based on the molecular docking analysis and the infection analysis in mutants. Less drug resistance tendency to PAO1 was observed, at least 20 generations tested. Furthermore, 4-Imidazolecarboxaldehyde could enhance the sensitivity of tetracycline and azithromycin to PAO1 obviously. Therefore 4-imidazolecarboxaldehyde was identified as a promising QSI agent of PA targeting las and rhl systems, used independently or synergistically with tetracycline and azithromycin to attenuate PA infections without obviously detectable resistance.

title: Antimicrobial stewardship and resistance in intensive care units in the UK: a prospective national audit
abstract: Principles of effective antimicrobial stewardship include prescription of empiric therapy based on the most likely causative organism, with medication review within 72 h. Adherence to best practice in UK ICUs is unknown and the aim of this study was to evaluate patient- and unit-level antimicrobial use in UK ICUs. We conducted a prospective national audit of antimicrobial use in adults (aged ≥ 18 y) admitted to ICUs in the UK and Isle of Man with a point-prevalence survey. Subsequently, we collected longitudinal data on review of therapy and antimicrobial resistance in a subset of patients who had commenced therapy within the previous 3 days. We studied 2626 patients from 154/292 (52.7%) ICUs. Antimicrobial therapy was prescribed in 1592 (60.6%) patients. Of 2116 empiric antimicrobial orders, 1592 (75.2%) were compliant with unit-level guidelines. For non-compliant orders, 253 (12.0% of all empiric orders) were discussed with infection specialists and 69 (3.3%) provided justification for off-guidance therapy, but 202 (9.5%) were prescribed outside guidance without justification or discussion with infection specialists. Guideline-compliant review within 72 h of prescription took place in 1488/1606 (92.7%) eligible medication orders. A pre-specified stop or review date was strongly associated with antimicrobial review within 72 h (adjusted OR 9.3, 95%CI 5.4-16.2). We have benchmarked critical care antimicrobial stewardship and guideline compliance across the UK. We recommend that pre-specified review dates are added to all prescriptions, as the most important determinant of review identified in our audit. Future work should include national stewardship audit cycles to benchmark practice and inform quality improvement initiatives.

title: Gold Nanoparticle-Based Optical Sensors for Antibiotic Detection: Recent Advances in Sensing Mechanisms, Portable Platforms, and Commercialization Prospects
abstract: The widespread use of antibiotics in various fields has resulted in rising contamination of environmental and food systems. Antibiotic residues accumulation poses serious risks like antimicrobial resistance, ecological imbalance, allergic reactions, and long term toxicity. Consequently, the accurate and precise quantification of antibiotic ion various samples are very important. Gold nanoparticles (AuNPs) have unique properties and emerged as one of the most promising nanomaterials having extensive application in various fields. This review comprehensively summarizes recent advances in AuNPs based optical sensors for quantification of antibiotics. At first, the fundamental optical and physicochemical properties of AuNPs are discussed, followed by an overview of surface modification strategies and molecular recognition approaches. Subsequently, the major signal amplification mechanisms including aggregation-induced plasmonic shifts, fluorescence quenching/enhancement, hot-spot engineering, catalytic amplification, and enzyme-assisted systems are critically examined. Recent progress in spectrophotometric, SERS, fluorescence, and chemiluminescence sensors is systematically reviewed with emphasis on sensing mechanisms, analytical performance, and practical applications. In addition, attention is devoted to portable and point-of-care sensing platforms such as paper based devices, lateral flow immunoassays (LFIA), smartphone integrated systems, wearable sensors, and microfluidic analytical systems. Comparative evaluation of different sensing approaches highlights their strengths and limitations regarding sensitivity, reproducibility, cost, portability, multiplexing capability, and commercialization potential. Finally, current challenges including nanoparticles stability, matrix interferences, reproducibility, regulatory approval, and large-scale production are discussed together with future perspectives focusing on artificial intelligence assisted sensing, multifunctional nanostructures, integrated microfluidics, and next-generation smart diagnostic systems.

title: Capturing the value of antimicrobial resistance innovation
Development of a TaqMan real-time PCR assay for the detection of the apramycin resistance gene aac(3)-IV in swine pathogenic Escherichia coli
abstract: We developed a TaqMan real-time PCR assay for detecting aac(3)-IV in cultured Escherichia coli isolates. The assay detected 10 CFU per reaction. All 114 apramycin-resistant isolates were PCR-positive, whereas all 1594 susceptible isolates were PCR-negative, demonstrating the assay's utility for rapid detection of aac(3)-IV in cultured isolates.

title: Trajectories of Antibiotic Consumption and Associations with Resistance Across Hospitals and Primary Care: A Population-Level Ecological Study in Shandong Province, China, 2012-2024
abstract: To examine antibiotic consumption patterns and their associations with resistance in hospitals and primary healthcare facilities (PHFs) in Shandong Province to inform antimicrobial stewardship (AMS). Yearly antibiotic consumption (2012-2024) and resistance (2014-2024) data for six resistance phenotypes were obtained in Shandong (population >100 million). Antibiotics were classified using the WHO Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical and AWaRe classification, with expressed as defined daily doses per 1,000 inhabitants per day (DID) and per 1,000 patient visits per day. Consumption structure was assessed using the Shannon index and Gini coefficient. Associations with resistance were examined using Spearman's rank correlation. Total antibiotic consumption decreased by 17.7%, from 11.98 DID in 2012 to 9.86 DID in 2024. Both hospitals and PHFs showed declining diversity and increasing concentration of consumption. Hospitals accounted for 27.7% of total antibiotic consumption, with increasing intensity and a shift towards fluoroquinolones and third-generation cephalosporins, whereas PHFs showed a marked decline and a shift towards extended-spectrum penicillins. Access antibiotics accounted for 27.0% in hospitals and 46.5% in PHFs in 2024. Ecological analyses showed broadly aligned consumption-resistance trends in PHFs, but divergent associations in hospitals. Antibiotic consumption declined in Shandong during a period of sustained AMS policies, but trends differed across healthcare settings. The alignment between primary care consumption and hospital-based resistance suggests that antibiotic use in PHFs may represent an important component of regional antimicrobial resistance dynamics. Future stewardship efforts should integrate consumption, resistance, and prescribing data to guide targeted interventions.

title: Risk factors for antimicrobial resistance in cancer patients and cancer survivors: An electronic health record study
abstract: To identify risk factors for antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in seven pathogen-antimicrobial combinations in patients with cancer and cancer survivors. Using data from patients with recent or past cancer diagnostic codes in Oxfordshire, UK, we examined associations between 22 potential risk-factors and AMR in blood culture isolates, collected between 1-April-2015 and 31-March-2025. Among 5975 bacteraemias in 4365 adults, we analysed 3141 (52.6%) due to Enterobacterales and 620 (10.4%) due to Enterococcus faecalis/faecium in 2752 patients. Fourteen risk-factors for antimicrobial-resistant bacteraemia were identified, varying across pathogen-antimicrobial combinations. Compared with no previous antimicrobial susceptibility test result, prior resistance to the same antibiotic in any culture in the last year was strongly associated with AMR across all pathogen-antimicrobial combinations (all p≤0.001). Prior antibiotic exposure and younger age were also positively associated with AMR in four and five combinations, respectively. Cancer type showed modest effects; haematological malignancies were associated with higher odds (vs colorectal cancer) of trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole-resistant Enterobacterales (aOR=2.07 95%CI 1.40-3.06) and vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus bacteraemia (aOR=6.68, 1.21-36.91). Previous resistance was the greatest risk factor for bacteraemia with AMR in cancer patients and survivors, with prior antibiotic exposure and age also contributing. Haematological malignancies increased risk of resistance to specific antimicrobials.

title: The Role of Diagnostic Tools in the Management of Ventilator Associated Lower Respiratory Tract Infections
abstract: Ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) remains a leading healthcare-associated infection in intensive care units and is closely associated with prolonged mechanical ventilation, excessive antimicrobial exposure, higher costs, and poor clinical outcomes. Despite decades of clinical trials and guideline development, bedside diagnosis remains limited by the absence of a biological reference standard. Conventional criteria combine nonspecific clinical, radiographic, and microbiological findings and cannot reliably distinguish parenchymal infection from airway colonization, endotracheal tube biofilm, or sterile pulmonary inflammation. Syndromic multiplex polymerase chain reaction panels, metagenomic next-generation sequencing, and host response profiling have greatly increased analytical sensitivity and shortened the time to microbiological information. They have also exposed the amount of microbial and inflammatory noise present in the ventilated airway. Detection of an organism, a resistance determinant, or systemic inflammation does not by itself establish causality. This review examines the strengths and limitations of clinical scores, imaging, respiratory sampling, conventional culture, rapid molecular assays, antimicrobial resistance testing, systemic and alveolar biomarkers, host transcriptomics, breath analysis, and artificial intelligence-based models. It proposes that VAP should be approached as a time-updated probability of tissue invasive infection rather than a binary diagnosis. A practical host-pathogen attribution framework should integrate the timing and trajectory of respiratory deterioration, specimen quality, relative pathogen burden and dominance, resistance and virulence signals, local and systemic host responses, prior antimicrobial exposure, and competing diagnoses. Diagnostic tests should be ordered only when a predefined management decision is linked to the result, followed by structured reassessment at 48 to 72 hours. This approach may improve antimicrobial targeting while reducing treatment of colonization and other noninfectious mimics.

title: Antimicrobial prescribing and guideline adherence in febrile inpatients in the Masanga Fever Study (MaFeStu) in Sierra Leone: a substudy within a prospective observational study
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance is increasing in sub-Saharan Africa, yet detailed data on prescribing practices remain scarce. We aimed to characterise antimicrobial compounds prescribed at admission, assess their concordance with treatment guidelines, and examine antimicrobial compounds prescribed during hospitalisation. We conducted a substudy of the Masanga Fever Study (MaFeStu), a prospective observational study of febrile inpatients at Masanga Teaching Hospital in rural Sierra Leone from Sept 26, 2023, to Sept 26, 2024. Patients aged 5 months or older who were assessed within 3 h of admission and had documented fever (tympanic temperature >37·5°C) or reported fever within the previous 72 h were eligible. Patients were excluded if study procedures would delay urgent care, and those without available medication records were excluded post hoc. Clinical data and diagnoses were recorded prospectively, and antimicrobial prescriptions were extracted from patient files after discharge. The primary outcome was concordance of antimicrobial compounds initiated at admission with the hospital protocol and WHO guidance, assessed using predefined decision rules. Prescribed compounds were also classified by WHO Access, Watch, and Reserve category and indication. Secondary analyses summarised antimicrobial compounds prescribed during hospitalisation, including oral step-down and culture-directed therapy. 689 febrile inpatients included in the analysis, the median age was 14 years (IQR 1·8-34·0), 358 (52%) were female, and race and ethnicity data were not collected. At admission, 487 (71%; 95% CI 67-74) patients received one or more antimicrobial compounds. Of 882 antimicrobial compounds prescribed, 573 (65%; 95% CI 62-68) were WHO Access antibiotics, and 309 (35%; 95% CI 32-38) were WHO Watch antibiotics. Ceftriaxone was the most frequently prescribed compound (268 [30%] of 882). Lower respiratory tract infections, sepsis, and skin and soft tissue infections accounted for the largest share of compounds prescribed, overall and within the Watch category. Overall, 650 (74%; 95% CI 71-77) of 882 prescribed compounds were concordant with the hospital protocol, compared with 491 (56%; 95% CI 52-59) under WHO guidance. Discordant prescribing under both guidelines was concentrated in common indications, particularly sepsis and lower respiratory tract infection. During hospitalisation, 58 (4·9%; 95% CI 3·8-6·3) of 1183 antimicrobial compounds prescribed represented oral step-down therapy, and 73 (6·2%; 95% CI 4·9-7·7) were culture-directed. Most prescribed compounds were WHO Access antibiotics and were largely concordant with hospital guidance and, to a lesser extent, with WHO guidance. Prescribing patterns suggest that strengthening diagnostics, refining treatment guidelines, and improving guideline familiarity could enhance guideline-concordant prescribing and antimicrobial stewardship in similar settings with constrained diagnostic and stewardship resources. Centre of Tropical Medicine and Travel Medicine, Amsterdam UMC, University of Amsterdam; Deutsche Gesellschaft für Internationale Zusammenarbeit/Klinikpartnerschaften.

title: Extended-spectrum β-lactamase-producing Enterobacter hormaechei and Klebsiella pneumoniae isolated from mammary and postoperative wounds in canine oncology patients
abstract: Extended-spectrum β-lactamase (ESBL)-producing Enterobacterales represent an increasing challenge in small animal medicine due to their limited treatment options and potential for dissemination in clinical settings. Although ESBL-positive Enterobacterales are increasingly recognized in dogs, their detection and clinical significance among dogs with cancer remain poorly investigated. Herein, we report the detection and genomic characterization of three ESBL-producing isolates recovered from wound samples of two dogs with neoplastic diseases. One Enterobacter hormaechei isolate was recovered from an ulcerated mammary tumor, whereas another E. hormaechei isolate and a Klebsiella pneumoniae isolate were recovered from a postoperative wound following thoracic nodulectomy. All three isolates were classified as multidrug-resistant and belonged to clinically relevant sequence types: E. hormaechei sequence type (ST) 114 and ST133, and K. pneumoniae ST11. All isolates carried bla, while K. pneumoniae ST11 additionally harbored bla. Genomic analyses also identified multiple virulence-associated determinants, including siderophore-associated genes in E. hormaechei ST133. To the best of our knowledge, this represents the first published report of E. hormaechei ST133 in a dog. These findings highlight the detection of clinically relevant ESBL-producing lineages in canine oncology patients and reinforce the importance of microbiological surveillance and antimicrobial susceptibility testing in veterinary practice.

title: A Comprehensive Study on Biofilm Formation Capability and Biofilm Associated Virulence Genes Carriage of Hypervirulent Klebsiella pneumoniae: Correlation between Biomass and Viability
abstract: Hypervirulent Klebsiella pneumoniae (hvKp) has drawn wide attention due to their distinctive features in virulence and pathogenicity. This study aimed to comprehensively investigate the biofilm formation capability and biofilm associated virulence genes carriage of hvKp. 552 K. pneumoniae isolates were isolated from various sources and identified to the species level, followed by antibiotic susceptibility test and correlation analysis among antibiotic resistance, clinical characteristics, risk factors, and invasive infection occurrence. Hypermucoviscous K. pneumonia (hmKp) and hvKp were further studied on serotyping, Multi-Locus Sequence Typing (MLST), biofilm formation and associated genes. We isolated 552 K. pneumoniae strains from various sources and 51 (9.2%) were identified as hmKp, with 26 and 25 sampled from invasive and non-invasive infections, respectively. Among the 51 hmKp, 43 (84.3%) were determined as hvKp, of which 25 and 18 were from invasive and non-invasive infections, respectively. ST23 and K1/K2 were the prevalent types in hvKp. High identification rate of biofilm associated virulence genes ycfM, entB, ureA, wabG was found. Importantly, approximately 65% and 85% of hmKp and invasive hvKp strains exhibit strong or moderate biofilm biomass and viability, respectively. Also, positive association between overall biofilm biomass and biofilm viability was found among 51 hmKp and 25 invasive hvKp. Remarkably, among both groups, strains with weak biomass tend to have weak viability, strains moderate biomass tend to have strong viability and strains with strong biomass tend to have strong viability, while strains with weak biomass rarely have strong viability. Comparative analysis revealed that kfu-positive, mrkD-positive, magA-positive isolates exhibited significantly higher biofilm biomass and viability, wabG and ureA showed no significant associations with biofilm phenotypes. This study has provided an important contribution to understanding biofilm formation capability in hvKp strains.

title: Microbiological and antimicrobial resistance profiles of shoulder, hip and knee periprosthetic joint infections: a 5-year retrospective single-centre cohort study
journal: Eur J Clin Microbiol Infect Dis
abstract: Periprost​hetic joint infection (PJI) is a serious complication of arthroplasty, and rising antimicrobial resistance complicates its management. We retrospectively characterised pathogens and resistance profiles of shoulder, hip, and knee PJIs within a five-year single-centre cohort. We included microbiologically confirmed shoulder, hip, and knee PJIs between June 2020 and March 2025, defined as: (i) at least two samples from tissue or tissue and synovial fluid positive for the same microorganism; or (ii) a single positive synovial fluid culture with a PJI-related diagnostic or surgical procedure code. We identified 239 PJI episodes in 200 patients, yielding 278 isolates; 208 episodes (87%, n = 208/239) were monomicrobial. Gram-positive bacteria predominated (88%, n = 244/278): Staphylococcus aureus and coagulase-negative staphylococci (CoNS) comprised 53% (n = 146/278) and were the leading pathogens in hip and knee PJIs, whereas Cutibacterium acnes comprised 59% (n = 44/74) of shoulder isolates. Gram-negative and anaerobic bacteria (12%, n = 32/278) were almost exclusively isolated from lower-extremity PJIs. No methicillin-resistant S. aureus was identified, but methicillin-resistant CoNS was common, particularly in knee PJIs. Conventional Danish empirical regimens (cefuroxime, cloxacillin) covered < 70% of hip and knee PJIs and ~ 80% of shoulder PJIs. For lower-extremity PJIs, only vancomycin-containing regimens combined with ciprofloxacin, piperacillin/tazobactam, or meropenem exceeded 90% theoretical coverage. For shoulder PJIs, all vancomycin regimens, including combinations with beta-lactams, achieved this threshold. PJI microbiology and resistance varied by joint, suggesting joint-specific empirical strategies. Danish beta-lactam regimens provided limited theoretical coverage, particularly for lower-extremity PJIs, driven by methicillin-resistant CoNS. Although clinical validation is needed, the findings support the value of local microbiological surveillance.

title: High prevalence of CTX-M-associated multidrug resistance and diagnostic accuracy of NG-Test CTX-M Multi among ESBL-producing Escherichia coli in Vietnam
abstract: CTX-M enzymes are the predominant extended-spectrum β-lactamases (ESBLs) worldwide, yet local epidemiology in Vietnam remains incompletely characterized. This study investigated CTX-M prevalence among ESBL-producingfrom inpatients at a tertiary-care hospital in Ho Chi Minh City and evaluated the diagnostic performance of the NG-Test CTX-M Multi assay. A prospective cross-sectional study was conducted at FV Hospital from January 2024 to April 2025. ESBL-producingflagged by the VITEK 2 Advanced Expert System (AES) were tested with NG-Test CTX-M Multi (NG Biotech, France). Antimicrobial susceptibility testing followed CLSI M100 guidelines (2024). Diagnostic accuracy was assessed against multiplex real-time PCR (Allplex Entero-DR Assay) in a blinded evaluation of 76 isolates. Of the 461isolates, 180 (39.0%) were ESBL producers; CTX-M was detected in 124 (68.9%). CTX-M-positive isolates showed significantly higher resistance to cefotaxime (98.4% vs 28.5%), cefepime (78.2% vs 10.7%), gentamicin (37.9% vs 12.7%), and ciprofloxacin (74.8% vs 73.2%); all< 0.05. Carbapenems and amikacin retained high susceptibility (>95%) in both groups. CTX-M-positive isolates exhibited broader resistance profiles (≥6 antimicrobial classes: 68.9% vs 27.8%). AmpC flagging was more frequent in CTX-M-negative isolates (69.6% vs 28.2%;< 0.001). NG-Test CTX-M Multi demonstrated 92.1% sensitivity (95% confidence interval [CI], 79.2-97.3), 94.7% specificity (95% CI, 82.7-98.5), PPV 94.6%, and NPV 92.3%. CTX-M was the dominant ESBL mechanism and was associated with broader multidrug resistance. NG-Test CTX-M Multi showed high diagnostic accuracy, supporting its role as a rapid screening tool; however, larger validation studies are warranted.IMPORTANCEInfections caused byproducing extended-spectrum beta-lactamases (ESBLs) pose a significant challenge for clinical management because they limit the effectiveness of commonly used antibiotics. CTX-M enzymes are now well established as the dominant ESBL determinants worldwide; however, their local prevalence and associated antimicrobial resistance patterns continue to vary across healthcare settings. In this study, we investigated the prevalence of CTX-M-producingand their resistance profiles in a tertiary care hospital in Vietnam. Our findings demonstrate a substantial burden of CTX-M-associated multidrug resistance affecting both hospital- and community-associated infections. In addition, the evaluation of a rapid lateral flow immunoassay for CTX-M detection highlights its potential role as a practical screening tool to support timely antimicrobial decision-making and infection control efforts. Together, these results provide clinically relevant data to support antimicrobial stewardship and optimize the management of infections caused by resistant.

title: Draft genome sequencing of Burkholderia cenocepacia strain DC660 isolated from a chronically colonized patient with cystic fibrosis
abstract: We have isolated thestrain DC660 from a chronically colonized pediatric patient with cystic fibrosis to develop a bacteriophage-mediated decolonization treatment to improve candidacy for lung transplantation. Whole-genome sequencing revealed antimicrobial resistance genes, consistent with the multidrug resistance observed in antimicrobial susceptibility testing, as well as several prophage-associated regions.

title: Phage therapy reduces bacterial burden and inflammation in a neutropenic murine sepsis model caused by hyperinvasive carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae
abstract: is an emerging opportunistic pathogen associated with severe clinical outcomes, and carbapenem-resistant(CRKP) has become a critical threat requiring alternative therapeutic strategies. Phage therapy has recently gained attention as a promising alternative to combat antimicrobial resistance. However, its efficacy alone and in combination with antibiotics in immunocompromised hosts remains understudied. Here, we established a cyclophosphamide-induced neutropenic murine sepsis model due to a hyperinvasive CRKP strain carrying multiple virulence factors., ceftazidime-avibactam (CAZ-AVI) at 8/4 μg/mL was required to suppress growth of this strain for 48 h, and this concentration was slightly reduced to 4/4 μg/mL when combined with a cocktail of three taxonomically distinct phages (P24, P39, and P49)., a single dose of the phage cocktail (9 × 10plaque-forming units/mouse), administered intravenously or intraperitoneally following bacterial challenge, achieved 2.5-5.1 logreductions of bacterial burdens across multiple tissues and organs. Correspondingly, serum tumor necrosis factor-α, interleukin-6, and interleukin-1β levels decreased significantly, and histopathological analysis revealed markedly mitigated inflammatory infiltration and tissue damage in the lung and liver. Both administration routes achieved comparable outcomes. Furthermore, in a delayed-treatment survival experiment, treatment with the phage cocktail combined with CAZ-AVI, initiated 2 h after lethal challenge, resulted in an 83.3% survival over the 28-day observation period. In contrast, all untreated mice succumbed within 2 days, and phage cocktail alone resulted in only 8.3% survival. Collectively, these findings provideevidence supporting the combination of phage cocktail and CAZ-AVI against CRKP infection in immunocompromised hosts. Carbapenem-resistant(CRKP) has emerged as a critical threat to global public health, causing life-threatening infections, disproportionately affecting immunocompromised patients who often fail to respond to conventional antibiotic therapy and experience high mortality rates. However, the efficacy of phage therapy in this vulnerable population and the comparative performance of different administration routes remain largely unexplored. Here, we established a cyclophosphamide-induced neutropenic murine sepsis model to evaluate the therapeutic potential of a phage cocktail against CRKP. We demonstrate that both intravenous and intraperitoneal phage administration achieve substantial bacterial load reduction and significant attenuation of systemic inflammation, revealing that phage therapy retains a robust positive response even in the absence of a fully functional host immune system. These findings underscore the clinical translational potential of phage as a viable alternative to antibiotics for combating CRKP infections in immunocompromised patients and provide critical evidence supporting intravenous phage delivery as a feasible administration route.

title: Genetic and Phenotypic Characterization of Listeria monocytogenes Isolates from Cattle Slaughterhouses in Korea
abstract: is a foodborne pathogen notable for its ability to persist in diverse environmental conditions and its genetic diversity across food and processing environments. This study aimed to characterize the genetic and phenotypic profiles ofisolates obtained from cattle carcasses and slaughterhouse environments in Korea. Between 2020 and 2022, a total of 36isolates were obtained from 8 of the 26 cattle slaughterhouses. Serotype 1/2a was the most prevalent (44.4%), followed by 1/2b (38.9%), 1/2c (8.3%), and 4b (8.3%). All isolates carried,,,,,, and, whileandwere detected in 97.2% andin 94.4% of isolates. In contrast,(pathogenicity island [LIPI]-3) and stress survival islet-1 were found in 41.7% and 50.0% of isolates, respectively, while(LIPI-4) was not detected. Pulsed-field gel electrophoresis analysis identified 16 different pulsotypes. Multilocus sequence typing identified 10 sequence types (STs), with ST324, ST8, ST224, and ST14 being the predominant types. These were grouped into eight clonal complexes (CCs) and classified into two evolutionary lineages: lineage I (CC5, CC6, CC224, and CC288) and lineage II (CC8, CC9, CC14, and CC121). Antimicrobial resistance analysis showed that all serotype 1/2b isolates were resistant to oxacillin, all serotype 1/2c (CC9) isolates were resistant only to tetracycline, while all serotype 4b (CC6) isolates were resistant to both daptomycin and oxacillin. These findings provide insights into the genetic diversity, virulence profiles, and antimicrobial resistance ofin cattle slaughterhouses and provide baseline information for improving hygiene practices and food safety management.

title: Impact of implementing an indication-based urinary tract infection diagnostic order menu at a veterans affairs facility
abstract: Inappropriate treatment of asymptomatic bacteriuria (ASB), particularly among patients with altered mental status (AMS), contributes to antimicrobial resistance and adverse outcomes. In June 2024, the Veterans Affairs Palo Alto Health Care System (VAPAHCS) implemented a required indication-based Urinary Tract Infection (UTI) diagnostic order menu, prompting indication selection for urinalysis with reflex to culture (UARC) or Urine culture (UC) orders. This analysis assessed the impact of the UTI diagnostic order menu on UTI-related clinical practice. Veterans aged 18 years and older with UARC or UC orders were included in this retrospective, quality improvement analysis comparing pre- (6/1/2023-11/30/2023) and post-order menu implementation (6/1/2024-11/30/2024) periods. Community living center (CLC) orders were excluded. The primary outcome was percent change of UARC/UC orders per month. Secondary outcomes included rates of UARC/UC order and therapeutic appropriateness, ordered vs. documented indication mismatch, AMS-related UTI diagnoses, and 30-day adverse outcomes (i.e., Clostridioides difficile infection, repeat UARC/UC order, and mortality). Data was analyzed using descriptive and chi-square statistics. Following implementation, UARC/UC orders decreased by an average of 30% over six months. One hundred orders were randomized to the pre- and post-implementation groups. UARC/UC ordering appropriateness improved significantly (61% vs. 85%, p=0.0004). There were no significant differences in treatment appropriateness or 30-day adverse outcomes. Only 8% of post-implementation AMS indication orders met criteria for likely UTI. The indication-based UTI diagnostic order menu significantly reduced UARC/UC orders and improved diagnostic appropriateness, supporting its role in enhancing diagnostic stewardship.

title: Electrocatalytic membrane-assisted chlorination overcomes the paradoxical increase in antibiotic resistance gene transformation risk
abstract: The horizontal transfer of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) via transformation is paradoxically increased under conventional chlorination. To address this issue, the suppression feasibility against ARG transformation was evaluated in an electrocatalytic membrane-assisted chlorination system (NaClO-EMs) using a laboratory-engineered Escherichia coli Top10 strain harboring pUC-blaTEM-1 as the donor. The NaClO-EMs system integrated CeOnanoparticle-decorated carbon nanotubes (CeO@CNT) electrocatalytic membranes with conventional chlorination and was operated in recirculation mode. The system reduced intracellular and extracellular pUC-blaTEM-1 abundance from 7.5 log to 2.3 log and from 6.5 log to 1.9 log, respectively. Consequently, transformation frequencies decreased to 3.1 × 10, with a further decline to 3.25 × 10after 24-h storage. In contrast, chlorination alone was associated with a 1.7-fold rise in transformation frequencies under identical storage conditions. Based on the physicochemical and physiological changes observed in the cells after treatment in the NaClO-EMs system, the suppression of ARG transformation may be largely attributable to three potentially synergistic pathways: (i) the reduced abundance, increased electronegativity and larger particle size of ARGs would reduce their cellular uptake; (ii) the reduced membrane permeability and elevated EPS secretion of donor bacteria would prevent their replenishment of environmental ARGs; and (iii) the suppressed motility, elevated intracellular oxidative stress, and depleted ATP reserves of recipient bacteria likely compromise their competence for ARG transformation. These findings demonstrate that the introduction of electrocatalytic membrane would effectively circumvent the transformation-risk paradox of conventional chlorination, offering a promising strategy for controlling antibiotic resistance dissemination in water treatment.
