abstract: Periodontitis is a bacterially driven inflammatory disease that can lead to tooth mobility and tooth loss. Conventional non-surgical therapy, antibiotics, and surgery may be limited by residual subgingival biofilms, antimicrobial resistance, and variable clinical outcomes. This review synthesizes recent studies of hydrogel-based systems for local periodontal therapy, focusing on stimuli-responsive release mechanisms, cargo-loading approaches, and regenerative outcomes in relevant animal models. Across these studies, hydrogels function as localized delivery matrices that can prolong retention at periodontal defects, regulate therapeutic exposure, and support tissue repair. We further evaluate translational considerations, including degradation behavior, long-termstability, and immunocompatibility. These findings position hydrogels as adaptable platforms for more precise periodontitis management and identify priorities for preclinical optimization before clinical translation.

title: Microbiota-constrained bacterial density limits phage infection in the gut and allows persistence of susceptible cells
abstract: With the rise of antibiotic resistance, bacteriophage-based treatments against bacterial infections have regained momentum. However, phage therapy has so far shown only moderate success in complex environments like the mammalian gut, where phages are particularly promising tools for microbiome engineering and specific elimination of opportunistic pathogens. Here, we use different murine models of intestinal colonization to quantitatively assess the minimal population size of susceptiblecells that is required for phage replication in the gut (replication threshold). We found that the composition of the intestinal microbiota is a key factor shaping phage-bacteria interactions by restricting the carrying capacity of susceptible host cells. We further demonstrate that the replication threshold enables coexistence of susceptible and resistant bacteria in phage-treated mice, with implications for phage-based applications in complex environments like the gut.

title: Exosome-Based Nanocarriers for CRISPR-Cas9 Delivery Targeting katGMediated Drug Resistance in Tuberculosis
abstract: Tuberculosis (TB), caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, remains a major global public health challenge, particularly because of the emergence and spread of multidrug-resistant (MDR) and extensively drug-resistant (XDR) strains. Mutations in the katG gene, which encodes the catalase- peroxidase enzyme responsible for isoniazid activation, are among the major molecular mechanisms associated with isoniazid resistance in M. tuberculosis. CRISPR-Cas9 technology has emerged as a potential approach for targeting bacterial genetic determinants of antimicrobial resistance. However, its therapeutic application against intracellular M. tuberculosis remains challenging because effective delivery must overcome both host-cell and bacterial barriers. Exosomes, a subclass of extracellular vesicles, have attracted considerable attention as potential biological nanocarriers because of their biocompatibility and capacity to transport nucleic acids and proteins between cells. This review examines the molecular mechanisms underlying isoniazid resistance, recent advances in CRISPR-Cas9 technology, the potential applications of exosome-based delivery systems, and the major challenges associated with their development for tuberculosis treatment. Unlike reviews that discuss CRISPR-based antimicrobial strategies and extracellular vesicle-mediated delivery separately, this review integrates these approaches to examine their potential application in targeting katG-associated isoniazid resistance in Mycobacterium tuberculosis. The review further evaluates the theoretical potential of extracellular vesicle-mediated CRISPR-Cas9 delivery for mutation- specific targeting of katG-associated isoniazid resistance, while considering the biological barriers that may limit its therapeutic application. Particular emphasis is placed on the need for mutation- specific correction rather than complete disruption of the katG gene, because loss of functional KatG activity can itself contribute to isoniazid resistance. However, the proposed exosomemediated CRISPR-Cas9 strategy has not yet been experimentally validated for targeting intracellular *M. tuberculosis*. Further in vitro, ex vivo, and in vivo investigations are required to establish its delivery efficiency, mutation-specific editing feasibility, safety, and potential therapeutic effectiveness.

title: Clinical Utility of Nanopore-Based Targeted and Metagenomic Sequencing for Rapid Diagnosis of Infections
abstract: Rapid diagnosis is critical for acute invasive infections, yet conventional culture is time-consuming. The real-time, long-read capability of nanopore sequencing facilitates rapid diagnosis, but standardized workflows are lacking. Here, we describe 2 nanopore sequencing workflows, nanopore targeted sequencing (NTS) and nanopore metagenomic sequencing (NMgS), for pathogen and antimicrobial resistance identification. A total of 176 residual clinical specimens, of which >90% were abdominal, pleural, joint, abscess, and bile samples, were analyzed using the NTS and NMgS workflows and compared with culture. NTS employed multiplex PCR to amplify 16S rRNA gene, internal transcribed spacer region, and 30 resistance genes, while NMgS involved host DNA depletion and unbiased sequencing. Among 152 culture-positive samples, NTS achieved 98.68% positivity, compared with 69.08% for NMgS. NTS identified 79.93% of cultured species, while NMgS detected 44.89%. For 24 culture-negative samples, NTS identified potential pathogens in 6 cases, whereas NMgS detected none. For antimicrobial resistance detection, NTS achieved a sensitivity of 84.62% for β-lactam resistance, 62.50% for quinolones, and 31.25% for aminoglycosides, with corresponding specificities of 87.10%, 75.86%, and 96.61%. Conversely, NMgS showed lower sensitivities of 36.84%, 16.67%, and 12.50% for these classes, while maintaining 100% specificity across all categories. Using the 4-h sequencing workflow, NTS and NMgS achieved comparable sample-to-report times (10.83 vs 10.41 h). This study demonstrates the potential of nanopore sequencing for rapid diagnosis and provides practical insights for its implementation in clinical laboratories. While NTS is sensitive and cost-effective, NMgS offers a hypothesis-free approach. These workflows may complement routine culture in specific clinical contexts.

title: Salmonella enterica strains differ in the effect of AcrABZ-TolC mutation on cell motility and susceptibility to bacteriophage Chi
abstract: The rise in multidrug-resistant pathogenic bacteria has renewed interest in phage therapy. The lytic phage Chi is a broad host-range phage infecting,, and. Chi belongs to the group of flagellotropic phages, which require a rotating flagellum to infect host cells. We previously reported that mutations in genes encoding components of the AcrABZ-TolC efflux pump greatly reduce Chi infection ofTyphimurium strain 14028S (serotype Typhimurium [STM] 14028S). Here, we tested and rejected the hypothesis that the AcrABZ-TolC complex is the cell-surface receptor for Chi. First, STM 14028S mutants with an inactivating point mutation in the AcrB pump displayed decreased susceptibility to Chi. Second, STM 14028S mutants of individual AcrABZ-TolC components showed reduced motility on nutrient soft agar, and a ∆mutant exhibited an over 80% reduction in the number of motile cells. Together, these results suggest that Chi phage resistance may be mediated by an effect on motility rather than by loss of a cell surface receptor. Additionally, deletions of,, andin another Typhimurium strain, STM 4/74, and two other serotypes, Choleraesuis and Poona, retained susceptibility to Chi and had no apparent motility defects. Taken together, mutations in the AcrABZ-TolC pump caused reduced motility and, thereby, Chi infection in STM 14028S, but not in other tested strains. These results suggest that this pump is not a cell surface receptor for Chi. Phage therapy is of rising importance for combating antibiotic-resistant pathogens. Particularly, phages targeting structures important for virulence are of interest as they present an exploitable evolutionary tradeoff, as bacteria will likely lose virulence to become resistant to the phage. We previously reported that inTyphimurium strain 14028S, the AcrABZ-TolC efflux pump, an important virulence factor, was also required for infection by the flagellotropic phage Chi. We report here that this requirement for Chi infection is due to reduced motility of mutants, rather than AcrABZ-TolC being the cell-surface receptor. The reduction in motility caused by AcrABZ-TolC mutations in strain 14028S is not conserved across other strains andserotypes, including Poona and Choleraesuis.

title: Anoxia selects for high-fitness biofilms and reduces antibiotic susceptibility in Pseudomonas aeruginosa
abstract: Antibiotic resistance is a growing global health crisis, yet resistance is almost exclusively quantified under aerobic laboratory conditions that fail to reflect the complex microenvironments bacteria encounter during infection. Many clinically important infection sites, such as airways of individuals with cystic fibrosis or chronic wounds, are microaerobic to anoxic. To address this, we investigated how anoxia alters antibiotic resistance determinants, hypothesizing that anaerobic metabolism might change the fitness effects and selection of resistance mutations. We used experimental evolution to propagatepopulations for approximately 200 generations under conditions differing in oxygen availability (oxic vs anoxic), growth mode (biofilm vs planktonic), and tobramycin exposure (subinhibitory increasing to inhibitory concentrations). Subinhibitory exposure reduced susceptibility to tobramycin by 2×-4× compared to ancestral levels, with anoxic populations consistently having higher minimum inhibitory concentrations than oxic populations. Mutations inandarose across all conditions, but mutations inwere only selected in oxic populations-indicating condition-specific mutations in response to antibiotics. Notably,mutations were observed in anoxic or tobramycin-exposed populations. Anoxic populations exhibited significantly increased biofilm formation, reduced twitching motility driven by type IV pilus gene mutations, and greater competitive fitness. Together, these findings demonstrate that oxygen availability shapes the response to antibiotics in, with the anoxic environment selecting for reduced antibiotic susceptibility, higher fitness, and high biofilm-forming phenotypes. is an opportunistic pathogen capable of acute and chronic infections that develop antibiotic resistance. One aspect ofthat makes it so challenging to treat is its metabolic versatility. We wanted to understand how growth in different infection-relevant conditions, specifically anoxia and surface attachment, would alter the evolutionary pathways of antibiotic resistance. We found that the mutations causing reduced antibiotic susceptibility to the commonly used antibiotic tobramycin were condition dependent. We also observed that adaptation to anoxia resulted inpopulations that had high biofilm-forming capacity and were highly fit compared to their ancestors. This indicates that anoxic infection environments can lead tovariants with increased resistance, increased recalcitrance, and potentially more virulence.

title: Quantification of antimicrobials and surfactants in drain biofilms: rapid extraction and comprehensive LC-MS/MS analysis
abstract: Biofilms formed in drain environments may act as reservoirs of chemical residues that contribute to the development of antimicrobial resistance. The occurrence of surfactants and antimicrobials in such biofilms remains poorly understood, partly due to the lack of studies jointly quantifying these compound classes. In this study, we developed a simple and robust sample preparation workflow together with a quantitative LC-MS/MS method for simultaneous analysis of diverse antimicrobials and multiple classes of surfactants in drain biofilms. The method showed reliable overall analytical performance in validation biofilm samples, with no notable interference observed for most analytes. Compound-dependent absolute recoveries, covering analyte losses during sample processing and ion suppression or signal enhancement in the MS, ranged from 22 to 111%. However, spike recoveries of 72 to 103%, obtained after normalisation with internal standards, indicate reliable and accurate quantification even for the compounds with low absolute recoveries. Application of the method tobiofilm samples revealed high concentrations of surfactant compounds, highlighting the necessity of compound-specific dilution strategies and individual internal standards. Overall, the method simplifies sample preparation and enables rapid multi-class quantification of disinfectants, surfactants and antibiotics in complex biofilm matrices, enabling improved assessment of their role in biofilm-associated antimicrobial resistance.

title: The complete genome sequence of an Acinetobacter baumannii phage, Djidily-mokiny
abstract: can cause life-threatening infections in immunocompromised individuals. Here, a bacteriophage with activity againstisolated from wastewater was sequenced. It has a genome size of 80,562 bp and represents a potential new genus of bacteriophage. It has no genes associated with lysogeny, bacterial resistance, or virulence.

title: Antibiotic heteroresistance observed across commensal Lactobacillus species
abstract: Lactobacilli are prevalent members of the microbiota in the intestinal and reproductive tracts of humans and other species. They are commonly used in probiotics due to their beneficial effects on human health, including their association with protection from numerous chronic diseases. In addition, these microbes are often prescribed to maintain their presence in the host during antibiotic therapy, as well as to treat diarrhea caused by antibiotics. Despite many studies examining the beneficial effects of lactobacilli, less is known about how they survive during antibiotic treatment, and in particular, whether they exhibit heteroresistance, a phenotype in which only a minor subpopulation of resistant cells coexists with a majority susceptible population. Here, we tested representativespecies for heteroresistance to a broad panel of relevant antibiotics. The results demonstrate thatstrains, including those isolated from human feces, can exhibit heteroresistance to relevant antibiotics from distinct classes, and are often heteroresistant to fluoroquinolones. In particular, heteroresistance to fluoroquinolones was even observed inGG, a widely used probiotic. These findings significantly impact our understanding of how lactobacilli, including strains isolated from human samples, can survive antibiotic treatment, and how individual probiotic strains may be selected for use during antibiotic therapy to promote their survival and maximize their benefits. Commensal bacteria, such asspecies, are widely used for their beneficial effects on gastrointestinal health and their potential to help restore the gut microbial community after antibiotic use. However, the antibiotic resistance profiles of these beneficial bacteria have received limited attention despite their relevance to probiotic use. Heteroresistance is a phenomenon in which a small subpopulation of resistant bacteria within an otherwise susceptible community survives antibiotic exposure, but it is often undetected, underappreciated, and has largely not been investigated among commensal bacteria. Our study provides a characterization of heteroresistance across distinctspecies and a panel of antibiotics, revealing that heteroresistance is far more widespread than previously appreciated, especially to fluoroquinolones. These findings suggest probiotic strains could be selected that would survive concurrent antibiotic therapy and thus highlight that more comprehensive resistance profiling of probiotic bacteria may yield benefits to patients.

title: Multi-target anti-Salmonella activity of metabolites from Piper aduncum against Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium: in vitro and in silico evidence
abstract: Salmonellosis is a major foodborne disease, and increasing antimicrobial resistance has intensified the search for new therapeutic agents. In this study, dillapiole and dihydroflavokawain B were isolated fromroots and evaluated for their anti-Salmonella activity againstserovar Typhimurium. Dihydroflavokawain B showed potent anti-activity (MIC = 12.1 µg/mL), while dillapiole exhibited moderate activity (MIC = 312.5 µg/mL). Molecular docking revealed favourable interactions with bacterial targets, especially for dihydroflavokawain B, which showed affinities comparable to reference antibiotics. In silico ADMET analyses indicated good oral bioavailability, intestinal absorption, and low predicted toxicity, highlightingas a promising source of anti-compounds.

title: 90-Minute point-of-care PRATHAMASENSE genosensor for gene-specific diagnosis of infection and antimicrobial resistance in critically ill patients: a multicentre diagnostic accuracy study
abstract: Infection remains a leading cause of morbidity and mortality when diagnosis and antimicrobial therapy are delayed. Standard culture testing requires 2-3 days for processing and reporting, forcing clinicians to initiate empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics - a major driver of antimicrobial resistance (AMR). We evaluated a novel point-of-care electrochemical DNA biosensor (PRATHAMASENSE Genosensor) against standard culture and molecular reference standards for the rapid detection of bacterial and fungal infections. In this multicenter, cross-sectional diagnostic accuracy study conducted over 12 months (April 2024-January 2025) at AIIMS Rishikesh and AIIMS New Delhi, India, we tested 488 clinical specimens (232 blood, 10 tracheal fluid, 246 urine) from patients with acute febrile illness, sepsis, or febrile neutropenia. Genosensor results were compared with the standard culture (primary reference standard) and, in a representative subset (n = 33), with quantitative PCR (qPCR). Bayesian latent class analysis (BayesLCA, R) was used to estimate sensitivity and specificity against an unobserved latent infection status, given the known imperfect sensitivity of culture. We did not collect clinical outcomes or treatment data because the study focused on diagnostic accuracy. Against culture, the PRATHAMASENSE Genosensor showed 93% sensitivity (95% CI 82.3-99.6%) and 77.8% specificity (95% CI 52.2-98.5%) in blood/tracheal samples, and 91.3% sensitivity (95% CI78.2-99.6%) and 77.6% specificity (95% CI 54.6-99%) in urine. When benchmarked against a combined sample of blood and urine of culture vs. PRATHAMASESNE Genosensor, the 94.2% sensitivity (95% CI 85.4-99.7%) and 88.3% specificity (95% CI 68.7-99.6%) were obtained using BCLA analysis. However, as a molecular platform, the sample was tested in parallel both in PRATHAMASENSE Genosensor and Q-PCR (Biofire and RT-PCR), showing quite interesting results PRATHAMASENSE against qPCR (n = 33), sensitivity was 93.75% (95% CI 69.5-99.8), and specificity was 94.12% (95% CI 71.3-99.8%). PRATHAMASESNE Genosensor-positive/culture-negative cases showed clinical and biochemical profiles similar to those of culture-positive cases, consistent with a high false-negative rate for culture rather than a Genosensor specificity problem. PRATHAMASENSE Genosensor delivers gene-specific detection of bacteria and fungi, including AMR determinants, directly from blood, tracheal fluid, and urine within 90 minutes - without a culture or PCR step. This point-of-care platform meets the WHO REASSURED criteria. This study assessed diagnostic accuracy only.
